title: Measuring forces with care: arrows, sagging lines and how sure a number can be

summary.text: A bottle that weighs only 5 newtons hangs in the middle of a washing line. Pull the line as flat as you can, and each end of the line pulls with 13 newtons or more. How can the ends pull harder than the whole bottle weighs? You will test this with a rubber-band gauge that you calibrate yourself, then ask how sure any measurement can be. You will also measure the hold of a water surface, which is only a few thousandths of a newton, and meet forces that change when things move.
summary.art: A 500 millilitre water bottle hanging from the middle of a thin line stretched between two chairs, a rubber-band gauge at one end, and small arrows along the line showing the pull.

intro.hook: Hang a heavy wet shirt in the middle of a washing line. Now try to pull the line so tight that the shirt does not dip at all. You can pull as hard as you like, and the line still sags. Why can you never get it perfectly straight?
intro.text: This looks like a small puzzle, but it hides a big idea. A force has a direction as well as a size. The same weight can need a small pull or a huge pull, depending on the angle of the line that holds it. In this unit, you will draw forces as arrows and measure the sagging line with a gauge that you test yourself. Then you will ask a harder question. How much can we trust any number that a tool gives us?
intro.art: A wet saree hanging in the middle of a washing line on a balcony, the line dipping in a gentle curve, and a child pulling one end with both hands.

outcomes: I can draw a force as an arrow, with the length showing the size and the point showing the direction.
I can find the net force when forces act along one line, and I can say what balanced forces mean.
I can explain why a line holding a weight must pull harder as it gets flatter, and I can test it.
I can calibrate a rubber-band gauge with a graph, and use the graph to read an unknown force.
I can repeat a measurement, show how much my readings spread and choose a typical value.
I can explain the difference between a reading error and a zero error, and between accurate and precise.
I can explain that a moving thing can pull harder or softer than its weight.
I can say how a digital scale measures force, and name one force far smaller than a newton and how it was measured.

terms.meaning: A drawing of a force. The arrow points the way the force acts, and its length shows how big the force is.
terms.example: If 1 centimetre stands for 1 newton, a 5 newton pull is an arrow 5 centimetres long.
terms.art: A hand pulling a bag to the right, with a 5 centimetre arrow drawn along the pull and a ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: The way something points or moves, such as up, down, left, right, forwards or towards a place.
terms.example: A pull to the left and a pull to the right can be the same size and still do opposite things.
terms.art: Two hands pulling a rope in opposite directions with arrows above each hand.

terms.meaning: Any measurement that needs both a size and a direction. A force is a vector. A length or a mass is not, because it needs only a size.
terms.example: '5 newtons' is not enough to describe a pull. '5 newtons to the left' is.
terms.art: A card saying 5 N with a question mark, next to a card saying 5 N with an arrow pointing left.

terms.meaning: What is left when you add up all the forces on one thing, counting opposite forces as take-aways. It tells you which way the thing will start to move, and how strongly.
terms.example: A cart is pushed right with 8 newtons and pulled left with 3 newtons by friction. The net force is 5 newtons to the right.
terms.art: A cart with a long arrow to the right and a short arrow to the left, and a middle arrow showing the difference.

terms.meaning: Forces that cancel exactly, so the net force is zero. A thing with balanced forces keeps doing what it was already doing.
terms.example: A book on a table has its weight pulling down and the table pushing up with the same size, so the book stays still.
terms.art: A book on a table with a downward arrow and an upward arrow of the same length.

terms.meaning: The pull along a rope, string or wire that is held tight at both ends.
terms.example: A washing line holding a wet shirt is in tension. Every part of it pulls on the next part.
terms.art: A taut rope between two poles, with small arrows along it pointing outwards at each end.

terms.meaning: The distance between the two places where a line, a rope or a bridge is held up.
terms.example: A washing line tied to two window grills 1 metre apart has a span of 1 metre.
terms.art: A washing line between two window grills with a measuring tape along the gap marked 1 metre.

terms.meaning: How far the middle of a line dips below the straight line between its two ends.
terms.example: A line that dips 10 centimetres in the middle has a sag of 10 centimetres.
terms.art: A line between two chairs with a ruler hanging from a straight stick above it, showing a 10 centimetre dip.

terms.meaning: The small mistake that comes from the way we read a tool. We can read a ruler or a gauge only to about half of its smallest mark.
terms.example: On a ruler with marks every millimetre, you can say 'about 5.5 millimetres', but not 5.52.
terms.art: A close-up of a ruler with a pointer between two small marks and a question mark.

terms.meaning: How far apart a set of repeated readings are, from the smallest to the largest. Scientists also call this the range.
terms.example: Ten readings between 4.7 and 5.3 newtons have a spread of 0.6 newtons.
terms.art: Ten dots in a row along a number line between 4.7 and 5.3, with a bracket over them.

terms.meaning: The reading we choose to stand for all the repeats. The middle value, when the readings are lined up in order, is a good choice.
terms.example: The readings 4.8, 5.0, 5.0, 5.1 and 5.3 line up with 5.0 in the middle, so the typical value is 5.0.
terms.art: Five numbered cards in a row in order, with the middle one lifted up.

terms.meaning: A mistake that is the same in every reading, because the tool does not start at zero. Repeating the reading does not remove it.
terms.example: A kitchen scale that shows 3 grams with nothing on it makes every weighing 3 grams too big.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with an empty tray showing 3 grams.

terms.example: A scale that reads 500 grams for a sealed 500 gram packet is accurate.
terms.art: A target with darts in the middle ring.

terms.meaning: Giving nearly the same reading every time, whether or not that reading is close to the truth.
terms.example: A scale that reads 508, 508 and 509 grams for a 500 gram packet is precise but not accurate.
terms.art: A target with darts bunched together in the outer ring.

terms.meaning: A graph made by testing a gauge with loads you already know, so that you can read the size of an unknown load from it.
terms.example: You hang 5, 10 and 15 newtons on a rubber band, plot the lengths and draw a line through them.
terms.art: A graph with load along the bottom and band length up the side, with a straight line through four dots.

terms.meaning: To find a value between two measured values by reading along the line you drew through them.
terms.example: A band 14 centimetres long lies halfway between the 12 centimetre and 16 centimetre marks, so its load is halfway between those loads.
terms.art: A graph with a dotted line going from a point on the side across to the line and down to the bottom.

terms.meaning: The pull along the surface of a liquid that makes the surface act like a thin stretched skin.
terms.example: A small steel needle laid carefully on water can float on this skin.
terms.art: A needle resting on the surface of water with tiny arrows pulling along the surface.

terms.meaning: A thin metal pattern stuck onto a piece of metal. When the metal bends a tiny bit, the pattern stretches, and its electrical resistance changes. A chip reads that change as a force.
terms.example: A digital kitchen scale has strain gauges stuck inside it.
terms.art: A zoom-in on a metal block with a zig-zag foil glued on it, bending slightly under a load.

terms.meaning: A huge scale set into the ground, big enough to weigh a whole lorry.
terms.example: A sugar mill weighs each lorry of cane on the way in and again on the way out.
terms.art: A lorry standing on a long steel platform with a small office beside it.

explanations.concept: A force has a size and a direction
explanations.definition: To describe a force fully, you need two things: how big it is and which way it acts. We draw a force as an arrow. The arrow points the way the force acts, and its length shows the size.
explanations.description: Suppose you say, 'I pulled the door with 20 newtons.' That is not the whole story. Did you pull it open or push it shut? A pull towards you and a pull away from you are the same size and do opposite things. So scientists always give a direction with the size, for example '20 newtons towards me'. A measurement that needs both a size and a direction is called a vector. To draw a force, choose a scale, for example 1 centimetre for every 1 newton. A 5 newton pull to the right is then an arrow 5 centimetres long, pointing right. A bag hanging from your hand has two forces on it. Its weight pulls it down. Your hand pulls it up. You draw them as two arrows on the bag, one pointing down and one pointing up.
examples: A 100 gram apple on your palm: its weight is a 1 newton arrow pointing down, and your hand's push is a 1 newton arrow pointing up.
Two people pulling a rope: each pull is an arrow, and the arrows point in opposite directions.
On a map, a wind of 20 kilometres an hour from the south is also a vector, because both the speed and the direction matter.
explanations.art: A school bag with two arrows drawn on it, a long one pointing down labelled weight, and an equal one pointing up labelled hand, with a ruler showing 1 centimetre for each newton.
explanations.context: You will draw many forces in this unit. This card explains why every force needs an arrow, and how to draw one.

explanations.concept: Forces on one line: add, take away or balance
explanations.definition: When forces act along one straight line, you add the ones that point the same way and take away the ones that point the opposite way. What is left is the net force.
explanations.description: In a tug of war, one team pulls the rope left with 400 newtons, and the other team pulls it right with 350 newtons. The rope moves left. The net force is 400 minus 350, which is 50 newtons to the left. If both teams pull with 400 newtons, the net force is zero. The forces are balanced, and the rope does not start moving. Balanced forces do not mean that nothing is happening. A book on a table has its weight pulling down and the table pushing up. Both arrows are the same size, and the book stays still. A bicycle at steady speed has the pedal push forwards and the air and road dragging backwards, also balanced. A thing with balanced forces keeps doing exactly what it was doing, whether that is staying still or moving steadily. A thing with unbalanced forces speeds up, slows down or changes direction. You can meet this idea again in the unit on changing motion.
examples: A cart is pushed right with 15 newtons and 25 newtons, and friction pulls left with 10 newtons. The net force is 15 plus 25 minus 10, which is 30 newtons to the right.
A skydiver falling at a steady speed has her weight pulling down and the air pushing up with the same size.
A bucket weighing 80 newtons is held still. Your hand pulls up with 80 newtons, so the forces are balanced.
explanations.art: A tug of war with 400 newton and 350 newton arrows, and a small arrow in the middle of the rope showing the 50 newton difference. Below it, a book on a table with two equal arrows.
explanations.context: You drew a force as an arrow. This card shows what happens when several arrows act on one thing along a line.

explanations.concept: Why a line can never be pulled straight
explanations.definition: A line that holds a weight in its middle must pull on its ends more strongly the flatter it gets. The pull in the line is only equal to the weight when the line slopes at 30 degrees. Flatter than that, the pull is bigger than the weight.
explanations.description: Hang a 5 newton bottle in the middle of a line. The line bends into a V shape. Each side of the V pulls up and sideways on the bottle. Only the upward part of each pull helps to hold the bottle up. The two upward parts must add up to the bottle's weight, 5 newtons. If the line is steep, each side has a large upward part, so it need not pull hard. If the line is nearly flat, each side points mostly sideways, and its upward part is only a thin slice of its pull. To get 2.5 newtons of upward part from a nearly flat side, the side has to pull very hard. Measure the sag of a line 1 metre long. A sag of 25 centimetres makes each end pull about 6 newtons. A sag of 10 centimetres makes each end pull about 13 newtons. A sag of 1 centimetre needs about 125 newtons. A perfectly straight line would need an endless pull. That is why no washing line can be pulled perfectly straight with a weight on it. Engineers use this idea when they build suspension bridges. They let the main cables sag, often by about one tenth of the span, because a flatter cable would need to be stronger and would pull its towers harder.
examples: A wet saree on a washing line makes the line dip, however hard you pull the ends.
A tightrope walker's rope sags where she stands, and the rope's ends are fixed to strong posts, because the pull on them is much more than her weight.
A suspension footbridge across a river has cables that sag in a gentle curve, not a straight line.
explanations.art: A bottle hanging on a line between two poles, drawn three times with the line steeper, medium and almost flat. Arrows at the poles get longer as the line gets flatter.
explanations.context: In the Sagging Line test, you measure the pull at the end of a line holding a bottle. This card explains why the pull changes.

explanations.concept: How sure is a number? Reading error and spread
explanations.definition: No measurement is exact. Every reading has a small reading error, and repeated readings spread out a little. To say how much we trust a number, we show the spread and choose a typical value.
explanations.description: Measure the same pull ten times and you will get slightly different numbers. Your eye sits a little higher or lower. The band is a little tired. The bottle swings a tiny bit. This is normal. It does not mean you are careless. The right thing to do is to measure several times and look at all the numbers. Line them up from smallest to largest. The smallest and largest show the spread, also called the range. The middle value is a good typical value. Suppose ten readings are 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 newtons. The typical value is 5.0 newtons and the spread is from 4.7 to 5.3, which is 0.6 newtons. We can write this as '5.0 newtons, give or take about 0.3'. It is more honest than one number alone. Also, do not write more digits than your tool can give. A gauge with marks every half newton cannot tell you 3.27 newtons.
examples: Ten children each read the same hanging bag on a gauge and get numbers within half a newton of each other.
A cricketer's bat speed, a doctor's blood pressure and a shopkeeper's weighing all come with a small give and take.
Scientists who measure the pull of gravity write numbers like 9.80 newtons for each kilogram, with a small 'give or take' printed after them.
explanations.art: Ten dots on a number line between 4.7 and 5.3, a bracket labelled spread over them and a tall arrow pointing at the middle labelled typical value.
explanations.context: In Ten Readings, One Pull, you repeat one measurement. This card explains how to talk about the numbers you get.

explanations.concept: Accurate and precise are not the same
explanations.definition: Accurate means close to the true value. Precise means giving nearly the same reading each time. A tool can be precise without being accurate, if it has a zero error.
explanations.description: Picture a target with a bullseye. If your darts all land close together in the outer ring, you are precise but not accurate. If they land all around the bullseye, you are accurate on average but not precise. If they land close together on the bullseye, you are both. A kitchen scale shows the same idea. Put a sealed 500 gram packet on it. If it reads 508, 508, 509, the scale is precise. It gives nearly the same number every time. But it is not accurate, because the true value is 500. It may have a zero error, which means it starts a few grams too high. A zero error is the same in every reading. Repeating the reading does not remove it, but checking the zero and subtracting does. A reading error is different. It is random, a little up or a little down, and repeating readings and taking the middle value does help. So there are two kinds of mistake, and each needs its own cure. Check against something known to find zero errors, and repeat to tame reading errors.
examples: A bathroom scale that always shows 1 kilogram with nobody on it has a zero error of 1 kilogram.
A cheap ruler printed a little too short makes every length too big, however carefully you read it.
Two careful children reading a gauge from slightly different eye positions get slightly different readings. That is reading error.
explanations.art: Three targets side by side: darts spread around the bullseye, darts bunched in the outer ring, and darts bunched on the bullseye, labelled accurate only, precise only, and both.
explanations.context: A scale can give the same number every time and still be wrong. This card explains the two different kinds of mistake in a measurement.

explanations.concept: A calibration graph: reading between the points
explanations.definition: A calibration graph is made by testing a gauge with loads you already know. A line through the points then lets you read the size of an unknown load. Finding a value between two known points is called interpolating.
explanations.description: A rubber band is not marked in newtons. But you can make it a forcemeter. Hang a known load, such as one 500 gram packet, which pulls with about 5 newtons. Measure the band's length. Then hang two packets, which pull with about 10 newtons, and measure again. Do the same for three packets. Plot the points on a graph, with the load along the bottom and the length up the side, and draw a smooth line through the middle of them. Now hang something unknown on the band and measure its length. Find that length on the side of the graph, go across to the line, and then go down to read the load. If the length falls between two of your points, you have interpolated. Be careful beyond your last point. A rubber band stops following a neat pattern when it is stretched a lot, so a guess past your last load is not trustworthy. A tool is only reliable inside the range where it was calibrated. A graph also tells you how good the gauge is. If the points fall on a line, the band stretches in even steps. If they curve, the steps get bigger or smaller, and the graph can still be used, because it follows the curve.
examples: Band lengths of 8, 12, 16 and 20.5 centimetres for 0, 5, 10 and 15 newtons. A band of 14 centimetres is halfway between 12 and 16, so its load is about 7.5 newtons.
A shopkeeper's spring balance has its marks printed from exactly this kind of test.
Scientists calibrate a new instrument by measuring things they already know, before they trust it on something new.
explanations.art: A graph with load in newtons along the bottom and band length in centimetres up the side, four dots and a line, with a dotted path from 14 centimetres across to the line and down to 7.5 newtons.
explanations.context: In the Sagging Line test, you turn a rubber band into a gauge. This card explains the graph that makes it work.

explanations.definition: The pull that a hanging thing puts on its support is equal to its weight only when the thing is still or moving steadily. A thing that is speeding up or turning can pull harder or softer than its weight.
explanations.description: Hang a bottle on a gauge. When it hangs still, the gauge shows its weight. Now lift the gauge quickly, so the bottle speeds up. For that moment, the gauge reads more than the weight, because the string must also give the bottle its speed. Lower it fast, and the gauge reads less. The same thing happens in a lift. When a lift starts to go up, the floor pushes you harder for a moment, and a bathroom scale under your feet would read more. When it starts to go down, it reads less. A swinging bottle shows it too. Let a 5 newton bottle swing down from the side, about 60 degrees from hanging, and at the bottom of the swing the string pulls with about 10 newtons. The bottle is not just hanging there. The string has to turn the bottle's path upwards, and that takes extra pull. A sudden jerk can be even stronger. Pull a cotton thread slowly and it holds. Jerk it, and it snaps, because for an instant the pull is far bigger than a steady pull would be. This is why engineers test bridges and ropes with moving loads, not only with still ones.
examples: A bathroom scale in a lift reads a little more as the lift starts going up and a little less as it starts going down.
A child on a swing pulls hardest on the chains at the bottom of each swing.
A bag dropped a short way and caught on a rope tugs much harder than the same bag hung gently.
explanations.art: A bottle hanging still from a gauge reading 5 newtons, and the same bottle swinging past the bottom with the gauge reading about 10 newtons.
explanations.context: In the Swinging Bottle activity, a moving bottle stretches the band further than a still one. This card explains why.

explanations.concept: Inside a digital scale: how bending becomes a number
explanations.definition: A digital scale measures force with a strain gauge. This is a thin metal pattern stuck on a metal block. The weight bends the block a tiny bit. The pattern stretches, and a chip reads the change in its electrical resistance as a force.
explanations.description: A spring balance shows force by how far a spring stretches. A digital scale does the same job in a different way. Inside is a block of metal called a load cell. When you put something on the scale, the block bends, by less than the width of a hair. A thin zig-zag of metal foil is glued on the block. When the block bends, the foil stretches slightly. A stretched foil is a little longer and thinner, and electricity finds it a little harder to pass through. A chip measures this tiny change and turns it into a number on the screen. The first practical strain gauges of this kind were made in the late 1930s. The same idea weighs a lorry on a weighbridge. Under the platform are several strong load cells, and the chip adds their readings. A sugar mill weighs a lorry of cane on the way in and again on the way out. The difference is the cane. Your phone has a tiny sensor of another kind. It holds a very small block on silicon springs, and it senses how the block moves, so it knows when you turn or shake it.
examples: A kitchen scale, a bathroom scale and a vegetable shop scale all use load cells.
A weighbridge at a sugar mill, a port or a mandi weighs lorries by measuring the bend of strong load cells.
A phone knows which way is down because a tiny block inside it is pulled by gravity, and its springs show how far.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a kitchen scale showing a metal block with a zig-zag strain gauge glued on it, bending slightly, with a wire to a small chip and the screen.
explanations.context: The forcemeters in school use a spring. This card shows what is inside the digital scales that you see every day.

explanations.concept: A water surface pulls: surface tension and a button on a balance
explanations.definition: The surface of water acts like a thin skin that pulls along itself. This pull is called surface tension. For water it is about 0.07 newtons for every metre of edge, and soap makes it smaller.
explanations.description: A steel needle laid very gently on water can float, although steel is denser than water. The needle rests on the water's skin. The particles of water attract each other. Inside the water, each particle is pulled equally in all directions. At the surface, each particle has water only on one side, so it is pulled sideways along the surface and inwards. The surface behaves as if it were a stretched skin. We measure it as a force along a length. For water, the force is about 0.07 newtons for every metre of edge. A flat plastic disc 3 centimetres across has an edge of about 9 centimetres. A water surface can hold it with about a hundredth of a newton at most, which is the weight of about one gram. In 1891, a German woman named Agnes Pockels measured this kind of pull in her kitchen with a button hung from a simple balance. She added weights to the other side until the button was pulled off the water. Soap makes the pull much smaller, which is why a soapy surface cannot hold a needle. This is also why soap helps wash things. The soapy water spreads and gets into small gaps.
examples: A drop of water on a leaf forms a bead, because its skin pulls it into a ball.
A water strider walks on the surface of a pond without sinking. She spreads her weight over the long edge of her legs.
Dropping a little soap on a water surface with floating pepper makes the pepper rush to the edges, because the surface pull is weaker in the middle.
explanations.art: A button resting on the surface of water in a bowl, with tiny arrows pulling outwards along the surface, hanging from the arm of a small balance with weights in the other pan.
explanations.context: How do you measure a force that is over a hundred times smaller than an apple's weight? This card shows a force that you can feel with your eyes closed, but only measure with a clever tool.

explanations.definition: Light carries a push. When sunlight lands on a surface, it presses on it with a very small force called radiation pressure. A big, thin, shiny sheet in space can be pushed by sunlight alone.
explanations.description: It is easy to believe that light has no push, because it has no weight. But light does carry momentum, and when it is absorbed or reflected, it pushes. In the early 1600s, the astronomer Johannes Kepler noted that comet tails point away from the Sun, and he is often said to have guessed that sunlight might be pushing them. In 1873, James Clerk Maxwell worked out from his theory of light that light must push. In 1900, Pyotr Lebedev in Russia measured it. In 1901, Ernest Nichols and Gordon Hull in the United States measured it too, with a twisting wire. The push is extremely small. Sunlight at the distance of the Earth pushes on a sheet of one square metre with only about five millionths of a newton, which is the weight of a grain of sand. But in space there is almost no air or friction. In 2010, Japan launched IKAROS, a spacecraft with a thin square sail, which used sunlight to push itself through space. In 2019, the Planetary Society's LightSail 2 used sunlight to raise its orbit around the Earth. The tails of comets, too, are blown by the Sun, mostly by a stream of particles from the Sun and by light.
examples: A solar sail is a very thin, very light sheet that catches the push of sunlight.
Sunlight on a square sail 14 metres on each side would push with about one thousandth of a newton, enough to move a spacecraft slowly but steadily.
The pressure of light inside a very big star helps to hold the star up against its own weight.
explanations.art: A thin square shiny sail with sunlight arriving from the left and a small arrow showing the sail being pushed to the right, with a comet tail in the background.
explanations.context: The tiniest force you have measured is a water surface's hold. This card goes to an even smaller force, one that comes from sunshine.

explanations.concept: A small magnet beats the whole Earth
explanations.definition: The electric force, which holds atoms together and makes magnets, is far stronger than gravity. A fridge magnet can hold a paper clip against the pull of the entire Earth.
explanations.description: The Earth has a mass of about six million million million million kilograms. Its gravity pulls the paper clip down. But a small magnet, held a centimetre above the clip, pulls the clip up and wins. That tells us something. Between two atoms, the electric and magnetic force is enormously stronger than the pull of gravity. Between two protons, the electric push is about a million million million million million million times bigger than their gravity. Gravity seems strong to us only because the Earth is so huge. All its atoms pull together, and there is no cancelling, because gravity only pulls. Electric forces come as both pushes and pulls, and in everyday things they cancel almost exactly. So what we feel as pushing and pulling, such as the stretch of a band, the grip of friction or the stiffness of a table, is the electric force at work between atoms. Scientists still do not know why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces. This is one of the open questions of physics.
examples: A magnet lifts a paper clip off a table, against the pull of the whole planet.
Your hand does not sink through a table. The electric push between atoms is much stronger than your weight.
A sheet of paper rubbed on hair can lift a tiny scrap of paper against the Earth's pull.
explanations.art: A small fridge magnet holding a paper clip upwards, with a huge Earth drawn below it and a small arrow downwards labelled gravity of the whole Earth.
explanations.context: You compare a magnet's hold with the Earth's pull in the Magnet Against the Earth activity. This card explains why the small magnet wins.

explanations.concept: Instruments made in India: Anna Mani and checking every copy
explanations.definition: A measuring instrument is only useful if every copy of it gives the same answer. So instruments must be built to a standard and checked against it.
explanations.description: Anna Mani was an Indian physicist, born in 1918 in Peermade in Kerala. She studied physics in Madras, and later, in London, studied the instruments used for measuring weather. After she came back in 1948, she worked at the India Meteorological Department in Pune. She is remembered for helping to make weather instruments in India, so that the country did not need to buy them all from abroad. Weather instruments measure forces and what forces do. A wind meter spins faster when the wind pushes harder. A rain gauge collects water to be weighed or measured. Instruments of this kind are placed in hundreds of stations, in places as far apart as hill towns and islands. For the numbers to be comparable, every copy of an instrument has to read the same when it meets the same wind or the same rain. So each one is checked against a standard before it is sent out, and checked again from time to time. This is the same lesson as the shopkeeper's scale and the kilogram standard. A number from one place can only be compared with a number from another place if both were checked against the same thing.
examples: Weather stations across India report wind, rain and sunshine, using instruments that have to agree with each other.
A new thermometer is checked in ice water and in boiling water, two places where the true temperature is known.
Legal Metrology officers check shop scales against standard weights.
explanations.art: A woman scientist in a workshop checking a cup-type wind meter beside a row of identical instruments waiting to be tested.
explanations.context: Who makes sure instruments agree with each other? This card tells about an Indian scientist who worked on this, and the lesson behind it.

explanations.concept: Is there one true value behind all the readings?
explanations.description: When we take ten readings of a pull, we usually imagine that there is one true size of the pull, and our readings scatter around it. Most scientists work with this picture. They try to get closer to the true value with better tools and more readings. But at the size of single atoms, quantum physics says something stranger. Some pairs of things, such as a particle's exact position and its exact speed, cannot both have sharp values at the same time. The more sharply you pin down one, the less sharp the other becomes. This is not a flaw in the tools. It is how nature seems to be. In physics, an observer means anything that takes a measurement, such as a detector. It does not mean a person or a mind. How this should be understood is still argued about.
examples: Ten readings of a bottle's pull on a band scatter around 5 newtons.
At the size of a single atom, the more exactly you fix where a particle is, the less exactly you can fix how fast it is moving.

perspectives.explanation: There is a true value, and good measurements get closer to it. The spread tells you how close you are.
For very small things, some measurable quantities do not have sharp values before they are measured. The spread is partly built into nature.
We only ever meet our measurements, not the thing itself. Whether a 'true value' exists behind them is a question that physics alone does not settle.

explanations.art: Ten dots scattered around a small cross on a number line, and beside it a fuzzy cloud with no sharp edge around a tiny particle.
explanations.context: Every set of readings has a spread. This card asks a deeper question: is there one true value hiding behind the spread, or not?

agreed.text: A force has a direction as well as a size.
agreed.evidence: Pulling a door open and pushing it shut use the same size of force and have opposite results. Scientists draw every force as an arrow for this reason.
agreed.context: This card is about why every force needs a direction as well as a number.

agreed.text: Forces along one line add up, with opposite forces taking away from each other.
agreed.evidence: Hook two forcemeters together and pull. Each shows the same number. Add a second helper on one side and the net force is the difference of the pulls, which matches how the thing moves.
agreed.context: This card is about how to find the net force on a thing.

agreed.text: A line that holds a weight in its middle pulls harder on its ends the flatter it is.
agreed.evidence: The rule is worked out from the angles of the line. For a 5 newton bottle on a 1 metre line, each end pulls with about 6 newtons at a sag of 25 centimetres and about 13 newtons at a sag of 10 centimetres, and a gauge at the end shows the same trend. Engineers use the same rule when they design cables and give suspension bridges a sag.
agreed.context: This card is about the sagging line, the main finding of the unit.

agreed.text: No measurement is exact, and repeated readings spread out a little.
agreed.evidence: Measure one pull ten times and you get several slightly different numbers. Every field of science reports measurements with a small give or take.
agreed.context: This card is about why scientists repeat measurements and show their spread.

agreed.text: A tool can only be trusted inside the range where it was checked against known things.
agreed.evidence: A rubber band follows a neat pattern for small loads and stops following it when stretched a lot. A forcemeter pulled past its range stays stretched and reads wrongly afterwards.
agreed.context: This card is about the safe range of a measuring tool.

agreed.text: The pull on a thing's support is the same as its weight only when the thing is still or moving steadily.
agreed.evidence: A bathroom scale in a lift reads a little more when the lift starts upwards and a little less when it starts downwards. A swinging bottle stretches a band further at the bottom of the swing.
agreed.context: This card is about why a moving thing can pull harder or softer than its weight.

agreed.text: Light pushes on what it hits, with a very small force.
agreed.evidence: Lebedev in 1900 and Nichols and Hull in 1901 measured the push of light on a hanging vane. Solar sails in space, such as IKAROS in 2010, have been moved by sunlight.
agreed.context: This card is about the push of light, which is far smaller than a newton.

challenging.claim: A line holding a weight only has to pull as hard as the weight.
challenging.who: Many people, who think that a support is as strong as the load it holds.
challenging.for: A hook holding a hanging bucket needs to pull up with exactly the bucket's weight. That is true when the support pulls straight up.
challenging.against: A line that slopes sideways pulls sideways too. Only the upward part holds the load. So a flat line has to pull much harder than the weight. In the Sagging Line test, a 5 newton bottle made the gauge read 13 newtons or more.
challenging.context: Do you think the ends of a washing line pull with the same force as the weight in its middle? This card looks at that idea.

challenging.claim: A tighter rope is a stronger rope.
challenging.who: Many people who tie ropes, and Murugan Anna in the story, before he changed his mind. It is a made-up character.
challenging.for: A slack rope sags, flaps and looks weak. A tight rope looks firm and strong.
challenging.against: Tightening a rope with a load on it raises the pull in it a lot. It is the pull in the rope that breaks it. A rope with a good sag, or a prop in the middle, pulls less and lasts longer.
challenging.context: Many people think a very tight rope is a strong rope. This card asks if that is true.

challenging.claim: If you repeat a measurement carefully, you should get exactly the same number every time.
challenging.who: Many students, and some textbooks that show only one clean result.
challenging.for: Machines that do the same thing again give nearly the same answer. A careful person should do the same.
challenging.against: Your eye position, a small wobble, a tired band and the way you hold the tool all change a little each time. Even the best instruments give a small spread. A set of readings with no spread at all usually means the tool is too crude to notice it.
challenging.context: You repeat a measurement in Ten Readings, One Pull. This card asks whether the numbers should all match.

challenging.claim: A scale that shows more digits is more accurate.
challenging.who: Many shoppers and buyers of gadgets.
challenging.for: Seeing 502.37 grams feels more exact than 500 grams.
challenging.against: The number of digits tells you how finely the scale shows its answer. It does not tell you how close the answer is to the truth. A scale with a zero error shows many wrong digits. Only a check against a known weight shows how accurate it is.
challenging.context: A digital scale can show a long number. This card asks whether a long number means a correct number.

challenging.claim: Your weight on a scale is always the same, wherever you stand and however you move.
challenging.for: On a quiet day, standing still, the scale shows the same number every time.
challenging.against: The scale really measures how hard you push on it. Bend your knees fast and it dips, then rises. In a lift that starts going up, it reads more. In a lift that starts going down, it reads less. On the Moon it would read much less.
challenging.context: You stand on a bathroom scale and read one number. This card asks if the number is a fixed fact about you.

challenging.claim: Light cannot push anything, because it has no weight.
challenging.for: A torch beam does not seem to move a feather. Light has no mass that we can weigh.
challenging.against: Maxwell's theory of light, from 1873, said that light must push. Lebedev in 1900 and Nichols and Hull in 1901 measured the push. The push is tiny, which is why we do not feel it. In space, with no air, sunlight can move a thin sail.
challenging.context: Can light push things? This card looks at an idea that seems sensible and turned out to be wrong.

challenging.claim: There is one true size of every pull, and good measuring finds it.
challenging.who: Most working scientists, as a useful way of working.
challenging.for: Better tools and more readings do tighten the spread. This lets us predict and build bridges that stand.
challenging.against: At the scale of atoms, quantum physics says that some quantities do not have sharp values until they are measured. Philosophers of science also point out that we only ever meet our measurements. Whether a true value exists behind them is still argued about.
challenging.context: Is there one true value behind a set of readings? This card gives the two sides of the argument.

big_questions.q: The line pulled harder than the bottle weighed. Where did the extra pull come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about the two ends pulling against each other, like a tug of war, with the bottle in the middle.

big_questions.q: Could a tightrope walker ever stand on a rope that is perfectly straight?
big_questions.hint: Think about the 1 centimetre sag in the table. What pull would you need?

big_questions.q: Ten careful readings gave ten different numbers. Which one is true?
big_questions.hint: Is any single reading the true one, or is the truth something we get closer to?

big_questions.q: If a scale always shows 3 grams too much, how could you ever find out?
big_questions.hint: You need a check that is not the scale itself. What could it be?

big_questions.q: A light beam can push a sail. Does it feel strange that light, with no weight, has a push?
big_questions.hint: What do we mean by 'push'? Is it about weight, or about changing motion?

big_questions.q: A small magnet beats the pull of the whole Earth on a paper clip. So is gravity strong or weak?
big_questions.hint: Compare two atoms. Then compare two planets. What changes?

big_questions.q: The water in a bowl pulls along its own surface. Is the surface a real thing, or a way of speaking about the top layer of particles?
big_questions.hint: Zoom in. Where exactly does the skin begin and end?

big_questions.q: Agnes Pockels was not allowed to go to university, but she measured something nobody had measured. Who gets to do science?
big_questions.hint: What did she need to start? A university, or a question, a button and a balance?

big_questions.q: A measurement is a number we make by comparing with something. Is a number a thing in the world, or a thing in our heads?
big_questions.hint: Did the 5 newtons exist before anyone had a unit called a newton?

big_questions.q: Every instrument changes a little what it measures. Can we ever see a thing exactly as it is when nobody is measuring it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the band that stretches when you hang a bottle. Does the bottle still hang the same way?

story.title: The Rope That Would Not Be Straight
story.note: A made-up story. The village, Thenmozhi, Mallika, Paati and Murugan Anna are imagined. The science is real. A line with a weight in its middle must pull harder on its ends the flatter it is, and a line with a good sag pulls less. Casuarina plantations really line the Tamil Nadu coast, and the northeast monsoon really brings rain from October to December.
text: Thenmozhi lived in a fishing village on the coast south of Chennai, where the sand was grey and the casuarina trees all leaned the same way, away from the wind. When the boats came in, the nets came out, heavy with seawater and weed. Her mother, Mallika, and the other women hung them to dry on a long rope between two tall casuarina poles at the edge of the village.

That October, the northeast monsoon arrived early. The nets never dried properly, and they stayed heavy. Three times in two weeks, the rope snapped in the night. Three times, a whole row of nets fell into the wet sand. Amma spent two days picking them out, knot by knot, with her lips pressed tight.

Murugan Anna owned the biggest boat on the beach, and he settled most arguments there. He looked at the broken rope and said, 'The rope was slack. A slack rope is a lazy rope. Pull it tight, and it will not fail.'

So the next day, six men tied a new, thicker rope between the poles. They looped one end round a stout stump and heaved on a wooden lever until the rope was as tight as a veena string. When Murugan Anna plucked it, it hummed. 'There,' he said. 'A rope that sings is a rope that holds.'

Thenmozhi was ten. She watched from the sand with her chin on her knees, and she saw something that nobody else was looking at. Even the tight rope was not straight. With a few nets on it, the middle dipped. And at home, Amma's washing line did the same. However hard Amma pulled it, one wet saree bent it into a gentle smile.

'Why can't it ever be straight?' Thenmozhi asked her grandmother that evening. Paati was sorting dried chillies on a mat. 'Ask the saree, not me,' Paati said. But she said it in a way that meant, go and find out.

So Thenmozhi found out. She tied a thread across the window of their hut, from one iron grill to the other. In the middle, she hung a plastic bottle of water. Near one end, she tied in a wide rubber band, because a rubber band stretches more when it is pulled harder. To turn the band into a gauge, she hung Paati's one-kilo packets of rice on it, one after another. She marked its length on the wall with a pencil. One packet, two packets, three.

Then she hung the bottle on the thread and began to pull the thread flatter. The flatter she made it, the longer the band grew. When the thread was only two fingers from straight, the band was longer than it had been with three packets of rice hanging on it. Yet the bottle weighed much less than one packet. She tried it again, and again, to be sure. Every time the band said the same thing. The flatter the line, the harder it pulled.

Thenmozhi sat back on her heels. The bottle had not become heavier. Only the angle had changed. The thread was not just holding up a bottle. It was pulling against itself, and the flatter it got, the harder it pulled.

Next morning the nets hung on the rope again, and the rope was singing again, and the sky was the colour of wet slate. Thenmozhi walked up to Murugan Anna with her bottle, her thread and her band. 'Anna, may I show you something?' she asked. Some of the men laughed. A girl with a rubber band!
Paati stood at the back with her arms crossed. 'Let the child show,' she said in her sharpest voice. Nobody argued with Paati.

Thenmozhi tied her thread between two posts of the drying rack and hung the bottle in the middle. She handed one end to Murugan Anna. 'Pull it flat, Anna,' she said. 'As flat as you can.' He pulled. The band near his hand crept longer. He pulled more. The band grew long and thin, and he stopped and stared at it.

'The bottle is small,' said Thenmozhi. 'But your thread is pulling harder than three packets of rice. A rope with all the wet nets on it is doing the same, to the poles.' Murugan Anna was quiet for the length of three waves coming in. Then he looked up at the rope between the casuarinas, humming in the wind with the nets hanging from its middle.
'It is not the nets that break the rope,' he said slowly. 'It is me, pulling it tight.' He turned to the men. 'Untie it.'

That day they tied the rope again, four hands higher on each pole, with a deep, lazy curve in the middle. They set a forked pole in the centre to hold it up, so each half carried half of the nets. The women laughed that the rope now looked like a smile. 'A lazy rope,' said Murugan Anna. And then, to everyone's surprise, 'A wise rope.'

The monsoon went on for six more weeks. Every evening the nets hung on the smiling rope, heavy as ever. Not once did it break. Thenmozhi kept her band on the wall of the hut, with its pencil marks for one, two and three packets of rice. Sometimes, when the wind was strong and the rope dipped a little deeper, she looked at it and thought of the thread across the window. The flatter the line, the harder it pulls. And nobody, however strong, can pull it straight.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a line with a weight in its middle is pulled upwards and sideways. Only the upward part of each side's pull holds the weight up, so when the line is nearly flat, each side must pull many times the weight. Pulling the rope tighter made the pull bigger, not safer. A rope with a good sag, or with a prop in the middle, pulls the poles and itself far less. Thenmozhi also did something scientists do. She made a gauge from a rubber band and checked it against loads she already knew, the rice packets.
ask: Why does a line that holds a weight pull harder on its ends the flatter it gets?
Why can nobody pull a washing line perfectly straight with a wet saree in the middle?
Two ways of making a line hold a heavy load while pulling less on its ends are to let it sag more and to add a prop in the middle. Why does each one work?
How can you turn a rubber band into a gauge for forces, and why does it need loads that you already know?
A rope holds in a light wind, but breaks in a gale. Why might the same rope have a bigger pull in it when the wind blows?

A thread tied across a window grill with a water bottle hanging in the middle, a rubber band near one end, and three one-kilo packets of rice hanging on the band, with pencil marks on the wall.

games.title: Net Force Showdown: which way does it go?
games.context: This is a card game about adding and taking away forces along a line. Each card describes the forces on one thing. Players say which way it will move and how big the net force is.

setup.art: A table with 24 cards in a face-down pile, eight direction tokens in a row, and a pencil and paper for each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: One child reading the front of a card aloud, while two players each put a direction token face down and write a number on a slip of paper.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Each other player picks a token and writes a number.

setup.art: The back of a card being read aloud, with the players turning their tokens over together and a score sheet beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Everyone turns over their token and their slip. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: forces on a thing on the front, and the net force on the back

items.f: A box is pushed right with 6 N and pulled left with 2 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 4 N to the right. 6 take away 2 is 4.

items.f: Two teams pull a rope. Team A pulls left with 300 N. Team B pulls right with 300 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The net force is 0 N, so the rope does not start moving.

items.f: A book weighs 8 N and lies on a table. The table pushes it up with 8 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. 8 N up and 8 N down cancel, so the net force is 0 N.

items.f: A bucket weighs 80 N. Your hand pulls it up with 80 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The net force is 0 N, so the bucket stays still or moves steadily.

items.f: A bucket weighs 80 N. Your hand pulls it up with 100 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 20 N up. 100 take away 80 is 20. The bucket speeds up upwards.

items.f: A bucket in a well weighs 80 N. The rope pulls it up with 60 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 20 N down. 80 take away 60 is 20. The bucket speeds up downwards.

items.f: Two friends push a cart right with 15 N and 25 N. Friction pulls it left with 10 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 30 N to the right. 15 plus 25 is 40, and 40 take away 10 is 30.

items.f: A trolley is pushed right with 12 N. Friction pulls it left with 12 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The trolley keeps doing what it was doing, still or at a steady speed.

items.f: A lift with its passengers weighs 8000 N. The cable pulls it up with 9000 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 1000 N up. 9000 take away 8000 is 1000. The lift speeds up upwards.

items.f: A skydiver weighs 700 N. The air pushes up on her with 700 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. She falls at a steady speed.

items.f: A parachute opens. The air pushes up with 1500 N. The skydiver weighs 800 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 700 N up. 1500 take away 800 is 700. She slows down.

items.f: A fan pushes a toy boat right with 3 N. The water drags it left with 1 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 2 N to the right. 3 take away 1 is 2.

items.f: You pull a drawer right with 5 N. Friction holds it with 5 N to the left. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The drawer does not start moving.

items.f: A cyclist pushes forward with 40 N. The air and the road drag back with 15 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 25 N forward. 40 take away 15 is 25. She speeds up.

items.f: A magnet pulls a nail up with 0.2 N. The nail weighs 0.1 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 0.1 N up. 0.2 take away 0.1 is 0.1. The nail jumps up to the magnet.

items.f: A hanging lamp weighs 7 N. Two chains pull it up with 4 N and 3 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. 4 plus 3 is 7, so the pulls cancel the weight.

items.f: Three children push a car right with 100 N, 150 N and 200 N. Friction pulls it left with 300 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 150 N to the right. 100 plus 150 plus 200 is 450, and 450 take away 300 is 150.

items.f: A ball falls. Its weight is 4 N down. The air pushes up with 1 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 3 N down. 4 take away 1 is 3.

items.f: A child sits still on a swing. She weighs 300 N. The chains pull up with 300 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The net force is 0 N.

items.f: A boat on a river is pushed right by the current with 500 N. A rope from the bank pulls it left with 500 N. What is the net force?
items.b: Balanced. The boat stays where it is.

items.f: You pull a rope right with 7 N. Your sister pulls it left with 9 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 2 N to the left. 9 take away 7 is 2.

items.f: A box is pushed up a slope with 50 N. Friction pulls it down the slope with 20 N. The slope's slant pulls it down with 25 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 5 N up the slope. 20 plus 25 is 45, and 50 take away 45 is 5.

items.f: A bag of rice hangs still from a spring balance that reads 10 N. What is the net force on the bag?
items.b: Balanced. The balance pulls up with 10 N and the weight is 10 N down.

items.f: A coconut falls from a palm. Gravity pulls it down with 15 N. The air pushes up with 0.5 N. What is the net force?
items.b: 14.5 N down. 15 take away 0.5 is 14.5.

printables.title: 8 direction tokens to show the way the net force points

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player is the reader. The reader turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. The back stays hidden.
Every other player picks one token for the direction. They also write a number in newtons on a slip of paper. They keep both hidden.
Everyone shows their token and their slip together.
The reader reads the back. The right direction scores 1 point. The right size scores 1 point.
For a balanced card, the token 'Balanced' with the number 0 scores 2 points.
After every 4 cards, the next player becomes the reader. With two players, swap after every card.
After all 24 cards, add up the points. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: read a card, choose your token, write your number, then check the back. There are 48 points to win. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards. Draw one arrow on paper with 1 centimetre for each 10 newtons, as a practice.
flow.say: Let us learn the game. A force has a size and a direction. Here is a 30 newton pull to the right. Draw an arrow 3 centimetres long, pointing right.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Draw an arrow for a 30 N pull to the right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Net Force Showdown. You set up the cards and practise drawing a force as an arrow.
flow.parent: One child with a parent works well: take turns being the reader, and swap after every card. With 3 to 5 players, nobody needs to be an adult. Cards can be copied by hand on small bits of paper if you cannot print.

flow.do: Play the first 4 cards slowly. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after the second card.
flow.say: I read the front. You pick a token for the direction and write the size. Now we turn them over together. What was your reason?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Write a number. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide the direction and the size?
good: I added the forces that point the same way and took away the other one.
The bigger force wins, and the net force is the difference.
They were the same size, so they cancelled and it was balanced.

flow.context: In this step of Net Force Showdown, you play the first four cards and learn how to find the net force.

flow.do: Play 8 more cards. Look for cards that say Balanced. After each balanced card, ask whether the thing is moving or still.
flow.say: This card is balanced. Does that mean the thing is still? Think about the skydiver.
flow.kid: Play 8 more cards. Look for the balanced ones. Is the thing still, or moving steadily?
flow.think: Can a thing be moving and still have balanced forces? Think of the skydiver and the cyclist.

check.q: A trolley is pushed right with 12 N and friction pulls it left with 12 N. Which is true?
options: It cannot be moving, because the forces cancel
It is still, or moving at a steady speed
It must be speeding up to the right
check.why: Balanced forces mean no change in motion. The trolley keeps doing what it was doing. It can be still, or moving at a steady speed. The first option mixes up 'no change' with 'no motion'. The last one forgets that the push is cancelled by friction.

flow.context: In this step of Net Force Showdown, you play more cards and see what balanced forces mean.

flow.do: Play the last 12 cards. Keep score. For any card you get wrong, draw the arrows on paper to see where the mistake was.
flow.say: Draw the arrows for the cards you missed. Put the longest arrow first. Which arrows point the same way?
flow.kid: Play the last 12 cards. Draw the arrows for any card you get wrong.
flow.parent: When a player gets a card wrong, ask them to draw the arrows rather than telling them the answer. Children often forget to count a force that points the opposite way. Drawing makes it easy to see.

check.q: Three children push a car right with 100 N, 150 N and 200 N. Friction pulls left with 300 N. What is the net force?
check.why: Add the three pushes to get 450 N. Then take away the 300 N of friction. 450 take away 300 is 150 N, to the right. The 450 N answer forgets the friction. The left answer takes the friction as the winner by mistake.

flow.context: In this step of Net Force Showdown, you play the last cards and fix mistakes by drawing arrows.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then pick the card that surprised you most, and say what you learned from it.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Which card surprised you the most, and why?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.think: If the net force is zero, where do the forces go? Are they gone, or still there?
flow.context: This is the last step of Net Force Showdown. You add up the points and think about balanced forces.

experiments.title: The Sagging Line: how hard does each end pull?
experiments.question: A 500 millilitre bottle of water weighs about 5 newtons. When it hangs in the middle of a line, how hard does each end of the line pull? Is it less than 5 newtons, the same, or more? And what happens when you make the line flatter?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When the line is almost flat, will each end pull with less than 5 newtons, exactly 5 newtons, or more than 5 newtons? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bottle, the same thread and the same rubber band gauge every time. Only the sag of the line changes. Measure the sag the same way each time, from the stick down to the thread. Read the band at the same place with your eye level with it. Do each sag three times and take the middle value, because one reading can be a fluke.

materials.item: a wide rubber band about 6 millimetres wide and about 8 centimetres long when relaxed, with no cracks. Keep 2 or 3 spare bands, because bands differ a lot
3 sealed 500 gram packets of sugar, dal or rice, as known loads of about 5 newtons each
a carrier bag with handles, to hold the packets
a 500 millilitre bottle of water with the cap closed tightly, as the weight on the line (about 5 newtons)
about 2 metres of strong plastic or jute twine (sutli) or thin nylon string, a paper clip and a pencil. Do not use sewing thread, which can snap, and never use kite manja, which cuts hands
a long straight stick about 1 metre long, such as a broom handle or curtain rod, two heavy chairs, masking tape and a soft cushion
a 30 centimetre ruler, squared paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Stand to the side and keep your face away from the band, in case it snaps. Never go past the 3 packet load. Stop if the band looks thin and pale. Keep the packets over a soft cushion, so that they do not land on feet. The thread under load can snap: keep faces and fingers away from the line, and hang the bottle over the cushion.
experiments.record: Write the band length for 0, 1, 2 and 3 packets. Draw the calibration graph. For each sag, write the three band lengths and the middle one, then read the pull from your graph. Last, write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you turn a rubber band into a gauge, then use it to measure the pull at the end of a line that holds a bottle. You see what happens as the line gets flatter.

setup.art: A long stick resting across the backs of two chairs and taped down, with a rubber band tied to the stick and a carrier bag hanging from the band holding a sugar packet.
setup.caption: 1. Make the rig. Hang a bag from the band and add the packets one at a time.

setup.art: A graph on squared paper with load in newtons along the bottom and band length in centimetres up the side, with four dots and a line through them.
setup.caption: 2. Plot the band length for 0, 5, 10 and 15 newtons. Draw the line.

setup.art: A thread tied to the left end of the stick and wound round a pencil at the right end, with the pencil held by the rubber band. A water bottle hangs from a paper clip on the thread.
setup.caption: 3. Hang the bottle on the thread. Turn the pencil to make the line flatter.

setup.art: A ruler held against the stick with the thread crossing it at 25 centimetres, and a second ruler beside the band measuring its length.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the sag with one ruler and the band length with another.

setup.art: A page with a table of sag and band length, the graph beside it, and three sentences written under it: claim, evidence and reasoning.
setup.caption: 5. Read each pull from your graph. Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

flow.do: Show your child the bottle, the thread, the band and the packets. Say that the bottle weighs about 5 newtons. Write their guess and their reason at the top of the page.
flow.say: This bottle weighs about 5 newtons. We will hang it in the middle of a line. Will each end of the line pull with less than 5 newtons, exactly 5, or more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A bottle weighs 5 N. It hangs in the middle of a line. Will each end pull less, the same, or more than 5 N? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think each end will pull with that much?
good: Each end holds half the bottle, so 2.5 newtons.
Each end holds the whole bottle, so 5 newtons.
A flat line has to pull harder, because it is pulling sideways.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children say 2.5 newtons, because the two ends share the weight. Write down whatever they say and the reason. One child with a parent: the child builds and reads, the parent turns the pencil and writes. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the stick steady, one turns the pencil, one reads the band at eye level, one writes. Swap roles for each sag. Every child writes their own guess first. A second rig is only needed if you want two groups to compare.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sagging Line test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Lay the stick across the backs of two heavy chairs, about 1 metre apart. Tape both ends down. Tie the band round the stick near the right end. Hang the carrier bag from the band. Measure the band's length with the empty bag.
flow.say: The stick holds both ends of our line. Tie the band near this end and hang the empty bag from it. How long is the band now? Measure from knot to knot, and write it down.
flow.kid: Lay the stick on two chairs and tape it down. Tie the band to the stick. Hang the bag. Measure the band.
flow.parent: The stick takes the sideways pull, so the chairs do not get dragged together. Tie the band round the stick twice so that it cannot slip. Measure the band the same way every time, from knot to knot, with your eye level with it. This is your 0 newtons length. Test the band before you start: stretch it by hand 10 times to loosen it. If three packets stretch it to more than about four times its relaxed length, or it looks thin and pale, use two bands side by side or a stronger one. If three packets hardly stretch it (under 1 cm), the band is too stiff to read; use a thinner, longer one.

check.q: Why do we measure the band's length from the same place every time?
options: So that any change in length comes from the load, not from where we measured
So that the band looks neat
So that the band stays cold
check.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If we measure from a different place each time, we cannot tell whether the band stretched or we measured differently. A neat band or a cold band does not affect the reading.

flow.context: In this step, you build the rig. The stick takes the sideways pull so the chairs stay in place.

flow.do: Put one 500 gram packet in the bag. Wait for the band to stop moving. Measure its length. Add the second packet, then the third, and measure each time. Then take all the packets out and measure the empty bag again.
flow.say: Each packet pulls with about 5 newtons. After each packet, wait until the band stops moving, then measure. Write down the length for 0, 5, 10 and 15 newtons.
flow.kid: Add one packet. Wait. Measure. Add another. Measure. Then take all of them out.
flow.parent: Now draw the graph. Put the load in newtons along the bottom (0, 5, 10, 15) and the band length in centimetres up the side. Plot four dots, and draw a smooth line through the middle of them. A ruler is fine if the dots fall in a line. If they curve a little, draw a gentle curve. When the packets come out, check that the band goes back to its 0 length. A band that stays long is tired. Use a fresh one.

check.q: On a made-up graph, a band is 12 cm for 5 N and 16 cm for 10 N. Your band measures 14 cm. About what pull is on it?
check.why: 14 cm is halfway between 12 cm and 16 cm. So the pull is halfway between 5 N and 10 N, which is 7.5 N. The answer 14 N mixes up centimetres with newtons. The answer 5 N picks the lower mark instead of finding the middle.

flow.context: In this step, you calibrate the band by hanging loads that you already know, and you draw the graph.

flow.do: Take the bag off. Tie the thread to the left end of the stick. Tie the pencil to the band, and wind the thread round the pencil. Slide a paper clip on the thread and hang the bottle on it. Turn the pencil until the sag is 25 centimetres. Measure the band. Then do 15 and 10 centimetres.
flow.say: Hang the bottle on the clip. Turn the pencil to make the line flatter. When the sag is 25 centimetres, measure the band. Do it three times. Then try 15 centimetres, and then 10 centimetres.
flow.kid: Hang the bottle on the thread. Turn the pencil to make a 25 cm sag. Measure the band. Do 15 cm and 10 cm.

ask.q: What do you notice about the band as the line gets flatter?
good: The band gets longer.
The flatter line makes the band pull more.
The band reads more than a bottle should, more than 5 newtons.

flow.parent: For a 1 metre line and a 5 newton bottle, expect about 6 newtons at 25 centimetres, 9 newtons at 15 centimetres and 13 newtons at 10 centimetres. Your span may differ, so your numbers may too. The clip should slide to the lowest point. If it sticks, tap the thread gently. Hold the stick still while you turn the pencil. Do not go flatter than 10 centimetres. If the band looks like it will go past the 3 packet length, stop. The graph cannot be trusted beyond that, and the band might snap. Read the band at eye level, three times for each sag, and take the middle value. The pencil is hard to turn when the line is tight. Wind several turns of thread on it, hold the turns with a finger, and tape the pencil to the band when the sag is right. Measure the sag after the band has stopped stretching, because the band lengthens a little as the line gets tighter. The pulls above are typical for a 1 metre span; in a damp or hot room a band may be softer, so always read your own graph, not these numbers. If the three sags give almost the same band length, the band is too stiff or the sags are too similar: use a softer band or try 30, 15 and 8 centimetres.

check.q: The band is longer than it was with 2 packets (10 N) when the line has a 10 cm sag. The bottle weighs about 5 N. What does this tell you?
options: Each end of the line pulls with more than 10 N, so more than the bottle weighs
check.why: The band is longer than with the 10 N load, so the pull is more than 10 N. This is more than the weight of the bottle, 5 N. The bottle has not changed. The flat line pulls sideways, and the pull needed to hold the bottle up gets bigger. A faulty band would not give the neat pattern across the three sags.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the bottle on a line, make the line flatter in three stages, and measure the band each time.

flow.do: Read each pull from your graph. Look at your first guess. Write three sentences: a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Draw one arrow picture, with two arrows pulling along the line and a short arrow for the weight.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did the numbers say? Why does a flatter line pull harder? Draw the two pulls along the line and the weight pulling down.
flow.kid: Read each pull from the graph. Was your guess right? Write what you think, what you saw and why.

ask.q: Why does a flatter line pull harder when it holds the same bottle?
good: A flat line pulls mostly sideways, so it has to pull more to get enough upward pull.
Only the part of the pull that points up holds the bottle.
The two ends pull against each other as well.

flow.think: Could you ever pull this line perfectly straight? What would the pull be?
flow.context: In this step, you read the pulls from your graph and write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: The Button and the Water: how hard does a water surface hold on?
experiments.question: A flat coin lying on the surface of water is held by the water. How big is the pull needed to lift it off? And does a drop of soap in the water change it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many grains of rice, added to a little pan, will it take to pull the coin off the water? Will soap make the number bigger, smaller or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same coin, the same bowl and the same balance every time. Dry the coin and balance the ruler again between tries. Only the water changes: first plain water, then water with soap. Do each water three times and take the middle value, because the coin sometimes tilts or pulls off early.

materials.item: a one-rupee coin, washed in soapy water, rinsed and dried, so that no grease is on it
a 30 centimetre plastic ruler, a round pencil and masking tape, for the balance
about 40 centimetres of thread and a small paper cup or a bottle cap, as the pan
a small blob of modelling clay, or a lump of atta dough, for balancing

400 grains of dry rice, such as basmati, a plate, and (if you can borrow one) a kitchen scale that shows grams. With no scale, use the typical 0.02 grams a grain, or ask a jeweller or kirana shop to weigh 300 grains
two wide bowls (one for plain water, one for soapy water), each with about 500 millilitres of water at room temperature, and 3 or 4 books and a few sheets of paper to stand a bowl on
a little liquid dish soap, a spoon and a paper towel

experiments.safety: Keep soap out of your eyes and wash your hands afterwards. Do not eat the rice after it has been used. Wipe up any spilt water so that nobody slips. Dish soap can sting eyes, so a parent measures the drops. Keep small rice grains away from younger brothers and sisters, and sweep up spilt grains.
experiments.record: Write how many grains weigh one gram, how many grains pulled the coin off the plain water and the soapy water, and the pull in newtons for each. Write one sentence for what the soap did.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you build a very sensitive balance and use grains of rice as tiny weights. You measure the pull of a water surface, a force over a hundred times smaller than an apple's weight.

setup.art: A pile of 300 rice grains counted into tens on a plate, and a kitchen scale showing about 7 grams.
setup.caption: 1. Count 300 grains in tens. Weigh them to find the weight of one grain.

setup.art: A ruler balanced on a pencil taped to a table, with a coin on a thread hanging from one end and a paper cup pan hanging from the other.
setup.caption: 2. Make the balance. The coin hangs from one end and the pan from the other.

setup.art: A bowl of water on a stack of books, with the coin just touching the water and level ruler above it.
setup.caption: 3. Raise the bowl until the coin just touches the water and the ruler is level.

setup.art: Rice grains being dropped into the paper cup one at a time, with the coin on the point of coming away from the water.
setup.caption: 4. Add grains to the pan one at a time until the coin jumps off the water.

setup.art: A drop of dish soap being stirred into the bowl, and the test being repeated with the same coin.
setup.caption: 5. Add soap to the water, stir gently, and repeat the test.

flow.do: Show your child the coin, the bowl, the ruler and the rice. Say that you will find out how hard the water holds on to the coin. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: A coin lying flat on water seems to stick. We will add rice grains to a pan until the coin comes off. How many grains do you think it will take? Will soap change it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A coin sticks to water. How many rice grains will pull it off? Will soap change it? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think soap might change the number?
good: Soap makes water slippery, so it holds less.
Soap makes the water thicker, so it holds more.
Soap does not change how water holds.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The usual answer is roughly 10 to 60 grains for plain water, and clearly fewer with soap. One child with a parent: the child drops the grains, the parent watches the coin and keeps the table still. With 2 to 4 children: one drops grains, one counts aloud, one watches the coin, one writes; each child takes one of the three tries on each water, so the three tries are done by three different people. One balance is enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Button and the Water test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Count 300 grains of rice onto a plate, in 30 piles of 10. Weigh them on the kitchen scale. Divide the weight by 300 to find one grain's weight. Write it down.
flow.say: Count out 30 piles of 10 grains. Now weigh them all together. If the scale shows 6 grams for 300 grains, how much is one grain? Divide the weight by 300.
flow.kid: Count 30 piles of 10 grains. Weigh them all. Divide by 300 to find one grain.
flow.parent: Long grain rice weighs about 0.02 grams a grain, so 300 grains weigh about 6 or 7 grams. A kitchen scale that shows only whole grams will round. That is fine. Use your child's own number. Count together, because it takes some patience.

check.q: 300 grains of rice weigh 6 grams. About how much does 1 grain weigh?
check.why: 6 divided by 300 is 0.02. One grain is about two hundredths of a gram. The answer 2 grams would make 300 grains weigh 600 grams. The answer 0.2 grams is ten times too big.

flow.context: In this step, you find out how much one grain of rice weighs, so you can use the grains as tiny weights.

flow.do: Tape the pencil to the table edge. Balance the ruler across it. Tie the thread to the coin with a tiny piece of tape, and hang the coin from one end. Hang the paper cup from the other end. Add clay until the ruler is level.
flow.say: Tape the pencil to the table. Put the ruler across it like a see-saw. Hang the coin on one end and the empty cup on the other. Add a little clay until the ruler sits level.
flow.kid: Tape a pencil to the table. Balance the ruler on it. Hang the coin and the cup. Add clay until it is level.
flow.parent: The coin must hang flat, like a tiny table, from its centre. Put a very small piece of tape on its top, and tie the thread to the tape. Check that the ruler is level before you add water. Place the bowl on books and slide it under the coin. Raise it until the coin just touches the water, with the ruler still level. If the coin hangs tilted, re-tape it nearer the centre. This step takes a few tries. Do not rush. Switch off fans and close the window, because a draught moves the ruler. Raise the bowl with books first, then fine-tune with sheets of paper under the bowl until the coin just touches the water. Stick the pencil to the table with tape so that it cannot roll.

check.q: Why do we level the ruler before the coin touches the water?
options: So that the only thing pulling the coin up is the grains we add
So that the coin gets wet evenly
So that the rice weighs more
check.why: If the ruler starts out level, everything on both sides balances, and only the added grains pull the coin. If it starts tilted, we would be measuring the tilt as well as the water's hold. Wetting the coin and the weight of rice are not the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you build the balance and set the coin on the water.

flow.do: With the coin touching the water, drop rice grains into the cup one at a time. Count aloud. Stop when the coin jumps off the water. Write the number. Dry the coin and level the ruler again. Do this three times.
flow.say: Add the grains slowly, one at a time. Count them out loud. Watch the coin. When it jumps off the water, stop and write the number. Dry the coin and do it again.
flow.kid: Drop grains into the cup, one at a time. Count aloud. Stop when the coin jumps off. Write the number.

ask.q: What do you notice about the numbers of grains from try to try?
good: They are close but not the same.
One try was much lower, maybe because the coin tilted.
They are around the same number.

flow.parent: Expect somewhere between 10 and 60 grains. Numbers that are close but not equal are normal. If one try is far from the others, the coin probably tilted or touched the water unevenly. Repeat that try. Keep the middle value of the three. What is typical, not promised: for a clean one-rupee coin, roughly 20 to 40 grains.
