If it comes off with fewer than 5 grains, the coin is greasy or tilted: wash it with soap, rinse, and dry it with a clean paper towel, and do not touch its face with your fingers. If 80 grains cannot pull it off, check that the thread is not touching the water and that the ruler was level.
flow.context: In this step, you add rice grains until the coin pulls off the water, and you do this three times.

flow.do: Add two or three drops of dish soap to the water. Stir gently with the spoon, and let the water go still. Dry the coin. Level the ruler. Repeat the test three times.
flow.say: Now we change one thing only. We add soap to the water and stir gently. We test again, three times. Does the coin need more grains or fewer to come off?
flow.kid: Add a few drops of soap to the water. Stir gently. Test the coin three times.
flow.think: Why might soap change the hold of water on the coin? What does soap do when it is washing a dish?
flow.parent: Soapy water is a bit slippery, so the surface pulls less and fewer grains are needed. Expect about half or fewer. If there is foam on top, skim it off with the spoon before the test. Use the second bowl for soapy water, so you can go back to plain water if a result looks odd. A damp or hot day does not matter much, but a dirty water surface does: do not touch the water with your fingers.
flow.context: In this step, you add soap to the water and repeat the test, to see if the hold of the water changes.

flow.do: Find the middle value for each water. Multiply the grains by the weight of one grain, to get grams. Multiply by 0.01 to get newtons. Compare with the 1 newton of an apple. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Take the middle number of grains. Multiply by the weight of one grain, to get grams. A gram pulls with about one hundredth of a newton. How does the pull of the water compare with the pull of an apple?
flow.kid: Find the middle number for each water. Change grains to grams, and grams to newtons.

ask.q: How many of these water-holds would make the weight of an apple?
good: About a hundred or more, because the water holds with about a hundredth of a newton or less.
Well over a hundred, because the water holds with only a few thousandths of a newton.
Soapy water would need even more.

check.q: The coin needed 30 grains of rice to come off plain water. One grain weighs 0.02 grams. What is the pull in newtons, if 1 gram pulls with about 0.01 newtons?
check.why: 30 grains times 0.02 grams is 0.6 grams. 0.6 times 0.01 is 0.006 newtons. That is about six thousandths of a newton. The answer 0.6 N forgets to turn grams into newtons. The answer 6 N is a hundred times too big.

flow.context: In this step, you turn your counts of rice grains into newtons, and compare the pull with an apple.

activities.title: Draw the Pulls: force arrows around the house

materials.item: 2 sealed 500 gram packets of sugar or dal, each about 5 newtons, and a carrier bag with handles
a school bag, a door and a drawer
squared paper, a ruler and two coloured pencils

schedule.what: Feel five forces. Draw an arrow for each one. Find the net force on each thing.

activities.record: A page with five pictures. Each has force arrows with their sizes, and a note saying whether the forces are balanced.
activities.context: In this activity, you feel five forces in the house and draw an arrow for each. You use the packets to tell you how big a newton is.

setup.art: A child holding a 500 gram packet flat on one palm, with a downward arrow 5 centimetres long and an upward arrow 5 centimetres long drawn beside the hand.
setup.caption: 1. Hold one packet. Draw its weight and your hand's push as two arrows.

setup.art: A hand pushing a door open and a hand pulling a drawer, with a long arrow on the door and a short arrow on the drawer.
setup.caption: 2. Push a door and pull a drawer. Draw the force arrows.

setup.art: A page with five small pictures, each with arrows in two colours and a note: balanced or net force.
setup.caption: 3. Draw all five. Mark the net force on each.

flow.do: Put one packet on your child's flat palm. Say that it pulls down with about 5 newtons. Ask what the hand must be doing to keep it still. Draw both arrows with 1 centimetre for each newton.
flow.say: Hold the packet still. It pulls down with about 5 newtons. What is your hand doing? Draw both forces as arrows, 1 centimetre for each newton.
flow.kid: Hold a packet still. Draw its weight as an arrow. Draw your hand's push too.

ask.q: How long should the arrow for your hand's push be, and why?
good: The same length as the weight arrow, 5 centimetres, because the packet is not moving.
It points up and it is the same size, so the forces are balanced.
Five centimetres, pointing the opposite way.

flow.parent: The weight arrow points down. The hand arrow points up and is the same length. Because the packet stays still, the two forces are balanced and the net force is zero. With 2 to 4 children: each child draws their own set of five pictures; take turns being the hand and the artist. A packet weighs about 5 N, so the arrow is 5 cm long on a 1 cm for 1 N scale.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Pulls. You draw the forces on a packet held in your hand.

flow.do: Ask your child to raise the packet slowly and steadily, then to snatch it upward quickly. Ask what the hand feels in each case. Draw the hand's push arrow longer for the snatch.
flow.say: Lift slowly. Now snatch it up fast. When did your hand have to push harder? Draw a longer arrow for the harder push.
flow.kid: Lift the packet slowly. Then snatch it up fast. When did you push harder?
flow.think: When the hand pushes harder than the weight, what happens to the packet?

check.q: A hand pushes a packet up with 7 N. The packet weighs 5 N. What is the net force?
options: 2 N up, so the packet speeds up upwards
check.why: The push is 7 N up and the weight is 5 N down. 7 take away 5 is 2 N up. A net force upwards makes the packet speed up upwards. The answer 12 N adds when it should take away. The answer 2 N down gets the direction wrong.

flow.context: In this step of Draw the Pulls, you lift a packet slowly and then fast, and compare the forces.
flow.parent: Put the packet in the carrier bag and lift it by the handles, so the packet cannot fly out. Guess before you lift: which will feel heavier, slow or snatched? Typical: the snatch feels like 7 to 10 N for a moment, though it is not measured.

flow.do: Push a door open slowly. Pull a drawer open. Draw an arrow for your push or pull, and an arrow for friction in the hinge or runner. Mark which is bigger.
flow.say: Push the door open slowly. You push one way. Friction in the hinge pushes back the other way. Draw both. Which arrow is longer, and how do you know?
flow.kid: Push a door open slowly. Draw your push. Draw friction pushing back.
flow.parent: If the door moves at a steady speed, your push and the friction are balanced. If it speeds up, your push is bigger. A drawer works the same way.
flow.context: In this step of Draw the Pulls, you push a door and pull a drawer and draw both forces.

flow.do: Hold the school bag by its strap. Try with 1 packet and then 2 packets in it. Draw the weight and the strap's pull for each case.
flow.say: Hold the bag with one packet, then with two. How do the arrows change? The strap's pull must match the weight to keep the bag still.
flow.kid: Hang the bag with 1 packet. Then 2 packets. How do the arrows change?

check.q: A bag with 2 packets weighs about 10 N and hangs still on a strap. How hard does the strap pull up?
check.why: The bag is still, so the forces are balanced. The strap's pull up equals the weight down, about 10 N. The answer 5 N is only one packet. The answer 20 N counts the weight twice.

flow.context: In this step of Draw the Pulls, you hang a bag and draw the weight and the strap's pull.

flow.do: Look at all five pictures. Mark each one as balanced or not balanced. Find the picture where the net force was biggest.
flow.say: Which pictures had balanced forces, and which did not? In which one was the net force biggest?
flow.kid: Look at your five pictures. Which are balanced? Which is not?
flow.think: A balanced picture does not mean nothing is going on. What is still going on in the balanced pictures?
flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Pulls. You sort your pictures into balanced and not balanced.

activities.title: Ten Readings, One Pull: how much do the numbers spread?

materials.item: a rubber band, a stick or broom handle, two chairs and tape, set up as in the Sagging Line test
a 500 gram packet of sugar or dal and a carrier bag
a 30 centimetre ruler, squared paper and a pencil
a second person who can read a ruler (a parent, a brother, a sister or a friend). Two or three more readers are welcome, but are not needed

schedule.what: Hang the same packet ten times. Read the band each time. Show the readings on a number line. Find the spread and the middle value.

activities.record: A table of ten readings for each reader, a number line with a dot for each, and a sentence giving the typical value and the spread.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure the same pull many times and see that the numbers are never quite the same. You find the typical value and the spread.

setup.art: A packet in a carrier bag hanging from a rubber band tied to a stick on two chairs, with a ruler held beside the band.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the packet from the band. Measure the band's length against the ruler.

setup.art: Three readers looking at the same ruler from different heights: from above, level and below, each with a different number in a speech bubble.
setup.caption: 2. Ask three people to read the same length, looking from different places.

setup.art: A number line from 11 centimetres to 13 centimetres with ten dots scattered along it and a bracket over them.
setup.caption: 3. Put every reading as a dot on a number line. Find the spread.

flow.do: Tie the band to the stick on two chairs. Hang the bag with one packet. Ask your child to guess how much the readings will vary, and why.
flow.say: We will hang the same packet ten times and read the band each time. Will we get the same number each time? How much will it vary? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We hang the same packet ten times. Will the numbers all match? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might the numbers be different if it is the same packet?
good: Our eyes are in a different place each time.
The band is not exactly the same each time.
It is hard to read between the marks.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. Many children expect all the readings to be identical.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Readings, One Pull. You guess how much the readings will vary.

flow.do: Hang the packet. Wait 10 seconds. Read the band to the nearest half millimetre. Take the packet off and rest the band for 20 seconds. Do this ten times. Write each reading.
flow.say: Hang the packet and wait until the band stops moving. Read it at eye level. Take the packet off and wait. Then do it again. Ten times in all.
flow.kid: Hang the packet. Wait. Read the band. Take it off. Wait. Do it ten times.
flow.parent: Read at eye level, at the same spot on the ruler, to the nearest half millimetre. Write every reading, even when two are the same. Do not throw away the odd ones. Typical spread is about 1 to 3 millimetres, but it depends on your band. If all ten readings come out exactly the same, that is a result too: the ruler cannot see the small changes. Then repeat with only 5 seconds of rest between hangs, and with a longer, softer band, to see if the readings now spread. The number 12.3 cm is an example, not what you will get.
flow.context: In this step, you take ten readings of the same pull. You write all of them down.

flow.do: Ask a second person to read the band while the packet hangs still. Then each of you reads it three times: once from above, once at eye level and once from below. Write what each of you reads. Compare.
flow.say: Now two helpers will read the same band. One looks from above. One looks from below. Do they read the same as you?
flow.kid: Ask two people to read the band. One looks from above. One from below.
flow.think: Is the band different for each reader, or is it the readers?

check.q: Three people read the same band and get slightly different numbers. What is the best explanation?
options: Each looks from a slightly different place, so the pointer seems to sit in a slightly different place
The band changes depending on who looks
Only the eye-level reader is real
check.why: When you look from above or below, the band's end appears against a different mark on the ruler. This is a reading error. The band is the same for everyone. All three readers are real. The reading at eye level is just the least affected.

flow.context: In this step, you see how looking from different places changes what you read.
flow.parent: Alone with a parent: the child reads, then the parent reads, and each moves their head to look from above and below. With 3 or more children, each child reads in turn.

flow.do: Draw a number line with a mark for every half millimetre. Put a dot for each of the ten readings. Find the smallest and largest. Subtract to get the spread. Find the middle value.
flow.say: Make a dot for each reading. Where are the dots bunched? What is the smallest? What is the largest? The gap between them is the spread.
flow.kid: Put each reading as a dot on a number line. Find the smallest and largest.

ask.q: Which number would you give as the answer, and why?
good: The middle number, because it sits in the middle of the dots.
The one where most dots are bunched.
I would give the middle and say how far the others spread.

flow.parent: Line the ten readings up from smallest to largest. The middle value sits between the fifth and sixth. Add them and divide by ten if you would like to find the mean. It will be close to the middle value. Show the answer as 'about 12.3 cm, give or take 0.2'.
flow.context: In this step, you turn your ten readings into a typical value and a spread.

activities.title: The Swinging Bottle: does a moving bottle pull harder?

materials.item: the rubber band and stick rig from the Sagging Line test, on two chairs
a 500 millilitre bottle of water with the cap closed tightly
about 50 centimetres of thread and a pencil
a soft cushion and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up releases the bottle. Keep faces and feet away from its path. Put the cushion on the floor underneath, in case the band snaps.

schedule.what: Hang the bottle still and mark the band. Swing it from two heights. See how far the band stretches at the bottom.

activities.record: A table with the band length for the bottle hanging still, and the longest length at the bottom of swings from a low start and a high start.
activities.context: In this activity, a bottle swings on a band. You see if the band stretches further when the bottle moves than when it hangs still.

setup.art: A bottle hanging on a thread from a rubber band tied to a stick on two chairs, with a pencil held still at the bottom of the band.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the bottle still. Hold a pencil at the bottom of the band to mark its length.

setup.art: The bottle pulled to one side and held, with a ruler showing how far the bottle is raised.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the bottle to one side and lift it by 10 centimetres. Hold it still.

setup.art: The bottle at the bottom of its swing, the band longer than before, with the pencil still marking the old length above the band's end.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. At the bottom of the swing, the band reaches lower than the pencil.

flow.do: Hang the bottle by about 50 centimetres of thread from the band. Let it hang still. Hold a pencil sideways at the bottom of the band, to mark where it ends. Ask your child to guess what will happen when the bottle swings.
flow.say: The band is long now, because the bottle weighs 5 newtons. When the bottle swings, will the band end higher, lower or at the same place at the bottom of the swing? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle hangs still. Mark the end of the band with a pencil. What will the band do when the bottle swings?

ask.q: Why do you think the band will end at that place when the bottle swings?
good: The bottle is still the same weight, so it will end at the same place.
The bottle is moving, so it pulls harder.
The band will bounce, so it will go lower.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. A grown-up should do the release in the next step. One child with a parent: the child watches and writes, the parent releases. With 2 to 4 children: one watches the band, one films, one writes, and the grown-up releases. Swap roles for each lift.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Swinging Bottle. You hang the bottle still and guess what swinging will do.

flow.do: A grown-up lifts the bottle sideways until it is 10 centimetres higher than when it hangs. Let go gently. Your child watches the bottom of the band, with the pencil still held in place. Do this three times. Then lift the bottle 25 centimetres and do it three times more.
flow.say: I lift the bottle to the side and let go. You watch where the band ends at the bottom of the swing. Is it higher, lower or at the pencil? Do we see the same each time?
flow.kid: Watch the band at the bottom of the swing. Is it below the pencil?
flow.parent: Expect the band to reach lower than the pencil at the bottom of every swing. The higher you lift the bottle, the lower the band goes. A 25 centimetre lift with a 50 centimetre thread is roughly 60 degrees, and in theory the pull at the bottom is roughly double the weight. Do not lift the bottle higher than this. A phone video in slow motion helps if you can see only a blur. The band also bobs up and down by itself, so watch only the first swing after you let go. Best method: stand a ruler or a sheet marked in centimetres behind the band and film in slow motion with a phone, then pause the video at the lowest point. If you have no camera, tape a small paper flag to the bottom of the band, and watch it against the ruler. The band may stretch only about 1 to 2 centimetres more than hanging still, so expect small differences. Use a calm room with the fan off.

check.q: At the bottom of the swing, the band is longer than when the bottle hangs still. What does this tell you?
options: The pull at the bottom of the swing is bigger than the bottle's weight
check.why: A longer band means a bigger pull. The bottle's weight did not change, so the extra pull is what the band must supply to turn the bottle's path upwards at the bottom. A tired band would not be longer in only the swings. The bottle has not got heavier.

flow.context: In this step, you swing the bottle from two heights and watch how far the band stretches at the bottom.

flow.do: Use your calibration graph from the Sagging Line test, if you have it. Read the pull for the still bottle and for the swings. Compare the size of the extra pull with the bottle's weight.
flow.say: Use the graph from the Sagging Line test. How many newtons was the band pulling when the bottle hung still? How many at the bottom of the biggest swing?
flow.kid: Use your graph. How many newtons when still? How many at the bottom of the swing?
flow.think: Why does the bottle pull harder at the bottom of the swing than when it hangs still?
flow.parent: If you have no graph, compare the lengths: the still bottle makes a certain stretch, and the swing makes a bigger stretch. A rough answer is fine.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the band lengths into newtons by reading them off your graph.

flow.do: Ask your child to say where else the pull is bigger than the weight. Think about a swing at a park and a lift starting up.
flow.say: Where else might something pull harder when it moves than when it is still? Think about a swing and about a lift.
flow.kid: Think of a swing or a lift. When does it pull harder than its weight?

ask.q: Where have you felt something pull or press harder when moving than when still?
good: On a swing, at the bottom, I feel heavier.
In a lift when it starts going up, I feel heavier.
On a bus when it turns, I get pushed.

flow.context: In this step, you find other places where a moving thing pulls harder than its weight.

activities.title: Magnet Against the Earth: how many clips can it hold?

materials.item: 50 or more steel paper clips of the same size

a fridge magnet. A thin, flexible rubber one is weak: use a thicker ceramic or steel-cased magnet (from an old speaker, a cupboard catch or a toy) if you have one, and, if you have one, a second magnet of a different size
a kitchen scale that shows grams, if you can borrow one. Without it, use the typical weight of a paper clip, about 0.5 grams
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Use only an ordinary fridge magnet. Very strong magnets, such as small shiny ones, can pinch fingers and are dangerous if swallowed. Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards. Paper clips are a swallowing risk for younger brothers and sisters, so pick them all up afterwards.

schedule.what: Weigh the clips. Hang a chain from the magnet. Count the clips it holds. Turn the count into newtons.

activities.record: A table with the weight of one clip, the number of clips each magnet held and the pull in newtons.
activities.context: In this activity, you use paper clips as tiny weights to measure the pull of a magnet. You find that a small magnet beats the pull of the whole Earth on the clips.

setup.art: A pile of 50 paper clips on a kitchen scale showing about 25 grams.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh 50 clips to find how much one clip weighs.

setup.art: A magnet held against the edge of a table with a chain of paper clips hanging from it, each hooked to the next.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a chain of clips from the magnet. Add clips until the chain falls.

setup.art: A page with a table of the magnets, the number of clips held and the pull in newtons.
setup.caption: 3. Count the clips. Turn the count into newtons.

flow.do: Weigh 50 paper clips on the kitchen scale. Divide the weight by 50 to find one clip. Write it down. Ask your child to guess how many clips the magnet will hold.
flow.say: A paper clip is very light. We weigh 50 of them and divide by 50. Then guess: how many clips in a chain can this magnet hold? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Weigh 50 clips. Divide by 50. Guess how many clips the magnet can hold.
flow.parent: A standard clip weighs about half a gram, so 50 clips weigh around 25 grams. Use your own scale's number. A kitchen scale that shows only whole grams is fine.

ask.q: How many clips do you think the magnet will hold, and why?
good: About ten, because the magnet is small.
Lots, because magnets are strong.
Only a few, because each clip has to be held by the one above.

flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Against the Earth. You weigh the clips and guess.

flow.do: Hold the magnet in your hand with its flat face pointing down. Touch it to a clip and hook more clips into a chain, one by one, until it falls. Count the clips just before.
flow.say: Touch the magnet to one clip. Hook another clip to it, and another, one at a time. How many can it hold before the chain falls? Count them.
flow.kid: Hook clips into a chain from the magnet. Add one at a time. Count until it falls.
flow.parent: A thin rubber fridge magnet may hold only 1 to 5 clips in a chain, and a thicker ceramic magnet may hold 10 to 30 (typical, not promised). Try three times and use the middle count. If the first clip sticks poorly, try the magnet's other end. If the magnet holds only 1 or 2 clips, the small numbers are fine: compare magnets, not newtons.

check.q: The magnet holds a chain of 20 clips, and each clip weighs about 0.5 grams. What does the magnet's pull have to be, at least?
options: At least the weight of 10 grams of clips, about 0.1 newtons
At least the weight of 1 gram
Exactly zero, because the chain is still
check.why: 20 clips of 0.5 grams weigh 10 grams. 10 grams is about 0.1 newtons. The magnet must pull up at least as much as the Earth pulls those clips down. The answer 1 gram is too small. A still chain has balanced forces. It does not mean there is no force.

flow.context: In this step, you make the longest chain of clips that the magnet can hold.

flow.do: Repeat with another magnet, if you have one. Write the number of clips for each magnet. Then put 1 sheet of ordinary paper between the magnet and the first clip, count again, then try 2 and 3 sheets. Convert to newtons: clips times the weight of one clip in grams, times 0.01.
flow.say: Now we change the magnet. Which holds more clips? Turn the counts into newtons. Multiply by the weight of a clip, then by 0.01.
flow.kid: Test a second magnet. Count the clips. Turn the count into newtons.
flow.think: The whole Earth pulls every clip down. Yet a small magnet wins. What does that tell you about the two forces?
flow.context: In this step, you compare two magnets and turn the counts into newtons.
flow.parent: Guess first: will a sheet of paper make the pull much weaker? Typically each sheet removes a few clips from a strong magnet, which shows that the pull gets weaker as the distance grows. With 2 to 4 children, each child tests a different magnet, and the group compares.

activities.title: Be a Weighbridge: weigh twice and take the difference

materials.item: a bathroom scale (or a neighbour's)
a school bag packed with books, about 3 to 5 kilograms
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Weigh yourself with and without a bag. Subtract to find the bag. Check with a second method. If you can, visit a place with a weighbridge.

activities.record: A table with your weight alone, with the bag, the difference, and the bag's weight checked another way.
activities.context: In this activity, you weigh yourself twice, once with a loaded bag and once without, and use the difference to find the bag's weight. A weighbridge does the same for a lorry.

setup.art: A child standing on a bathroom scale holding a school bag, and the same child standing on the scale without the bag.
setup.caption: 1. Stand on the scale alone, then with the bag. Write both readings.

setup.art: A lorry of sugar cane on a weighbridge on the way in, and the same lorry empty on the way out, with two weights written on a board.
setup.caption: 2. A weighbridge weighs the loaded lorry and the empty lorry. The difference is the cargo.

setup.art: A page with the two scale readings and a subtraction.
setup.caption: 3. Subtract the two readings to find the weight of the bag.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how heavy the loaded bag is in kilograms. Write the guess. Then weigh the bag on the bathroom scale.
flow.say: Guess how heavy your loaded bag is. Then step on the scale with it in your hands. What does the scale show?
flow.kid: Guess how heavy the bag is. Step on the scale holding it. Read the scale.
flow.parent: A bathroom scale may freeze its first reading. Step on once more for each reading. A reading with the bag alone on the scale is also fine, if the scale can read small weights. Keep the bag to about 3 to 5 kilograms, so that a child can lift it safely. An analog scale shows only to the nearest half or whole kilogram, which is a coarse reading: then use a heavier bag, 5 kilograms, to see a clear difference. With 2 to 4 children, take turns: one stands on the scale, one reads, one writes. The readings of a digital scale are typically within 0.1 to 0.2 kilograms of each other.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be a Weighbridge. You guess and take the first weighing.

flow.do: Weigh your child alone, then holding the bag. Write both readings. Subtract the first from the second to find the bag. Compare it with the weight of the bag alone, if the scale can read it.
flow.say: First we weigh you alone. Then you hold the bag and we weigh you again. How do we find the weight of the bag from the two numbers?
flow.kid: Weigh yourself alone. Weigh yourself with the bag. Take away the first number.

check.q: You weigh 28 kg alone and 33 kg with a bag. About how much does the bag weigh?
check.why: 33 take away 28 is 5, so the bag is about 5 kg. The answer 61 adds the readings when it should take them away. The answer 33 forgets that the scale also weighed you.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh yourself twice and subtract to find the weight of the bag.

flow.do: Repeat three times with the bag. Ask your child to find the spread of the three answers. Ask why a lorry is weighed twice at the mill and not once.
flow.say: Do it three times. Are the answers the same each time? Now think about the lorry. Why is it weighed on the way in and on the way out?
flow.kid: Do it three times. Are the answers the same? Why weigh a lorry twice?

ask.q: Why does a weighbridge weigh a lorry twice?
good: The lorry itself is heavy, so it has to be weighed without the cargo.
The difference is the weight of the cargo.
One weighing would add the weight of the lorry to the cargo.

flow.context: In this step, you repeat the weighing and see why a weighbridge does it twice.

flow.do: If a weighbridge is near you, ask a grown-up to take you to watch from a safe place. It might be at a mill, a mandi, a port or a steel yard. Notice the platform, the office and the display. Ask what the scale can weigh.
flow.say: If you can visit a weighbridge, look at the platform and the office. Ask how many tonnes it can weigh and who checks it. Outside, stay with a grown-up and keep away from the lorries.
flow.kid: Visit a weighbridge with a grown-up. Stay far from the lorries. Ask what it weighs.
flow.parent: Most weighbridges are in busy places with moving lorries. Stay well away from the platform and ask staff first. Look for the seal or stamp from Legal Metrology. If there is no weighbridge near you, a short video of one is a fine replacement.
flow.context: This is the last step of Be a Weighbridge. If there is one near you, you go and see a real weighbridge.

projects.title: The Bending Ruler Scale: weigh with a ruler that bends

materials.item: a plastic or thin wooden ruler about 30 centimetres long
a heavy book or two, and a table with a flat edge

5 loads of about 100 grams each (about 1 newton): small sealed 100 gram packets of tea, salt or sugar, or 100 millilitres of water in a small knotted plastic bag, measured with a medicine cup or 20 teaspoons
a small bag or a plastic cup with a loop of thread, to hang the packets on the ruler's tip

a second ruler or a tape to measure how far the tip bends down, squared paper and a pencil. A kitchen scale to check the answers is optional: otherwise use the weights printed on packets, or a kirana shop's scale
3 mystery objects to weigh, such as an apple, a steel tumbler and a pencil box

projects.safety: A ruler can snap if it is bent too far. Keep your face away from it. Stop adding packets if the tip bends more than 3 centimetres.

schedule.what: Build the ruler scale. Hang 1, 2, 3 and 4 packets. Measure the bend each time. Draw the graph.
Weigh three mystery objects with your ruler scale. Check each one against a kitchen scale.

projects.record: A graph of the bend of the ruler tip against the load in newtons, and a table of three objects with the weight from your ruler scale and the weight from the kitchen scale.
projects.context: In this project, you build a force meter from a bending ruler, the same idea as the load cell in a digital scale. You calibrate it and weigh three mystery objects.

setup.art: A ruler with 20 centimetres lying on a table under a heavy book and 10 centimetres sticking out over the edge, with a loop of thread and a small bag at the tip.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the ruler under a heavy book, with 10 centimetres sticking out over the table edge.

setup.art: The ruler tip bending down by 1 centimetre with a 100 gram packet in the bag, measured by a second ruler standing on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Hang one packet. Measure how far the tip bends down.

setup.art: A graph with load in newtons along the bottom and the bend in millimetres up the side, with five dots and a straight line.
setup.caption: 3. Hang 1, 2, 3 and 4 packets. Plot the bends and draw the line.

setup.art: An apple in the bag, the ruler bending, a dotted line from the bend across to the graph line and down to 1 newton.
setup.caption: 4. On day 2, hang a mystery object. Read its weight from the graph.

flow.do: Lay the ruler on the table with a few centimetres sticking out over the edge (see the note for how far). Put a heavy book on the other end. Ask your child to guess how many millimetres the tip will bend with one packet, and with four.
flow.say: A ruler is a springy stick. When we hang a weight on its tip, it will bend. If one packet bends the tip by 1 centimetre, how far will four packets bend it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A ruler bends when you hang a packet on it. Will four packets bend it four times as much?

ask.q: Why do you think the bend will grow in that way?
good: Four packets pull four times as hard, so it should bend four times as far.
The ruler might bend more and more, so it will be more than four times.
I do not know, so I will test it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The ruler must be held firmly, so press the book down hard. How much it bends depends on your ruler: a thin, bendy plastic one needs only about 4 to 6 centimetres sticking out, and a stiff wooden or steel one may need 20 centimetres or may be too stiff to use. Slide the ruler until one packet makes the tip drop about 4 to 8 millimetres and four packets drop it no more than about 3 centimetres. If the tip does not move at all, use a thinner strip. With 2 to 4 children: one presses the book, one adds packets, one reads the tip, one writes; each child brings one mystery object on day 2.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bending Ruler Scale. You guess how a ruler will bend.

flow.do: Hang the bag on the ruler's tip with its loop of thread. Measure how far the tip drops, with the empty bag. Add one packet. Wait until it stops moving. Measure the tip again. Write the drop from the empty bag.
flow.say: Hang the empty bag. Measure the tip's height. Add one packet and measure again. How much has the tip dropped?
flow.kid: Hang the empty bag. Measure the tip. Add a packet. Measure again.
flow.parent: Measure the tip from the floor or from a ruler standing upright by the tip. Be careful to measure at the same place each time. Millimetres are best. Take the bag's own drop away, and look only at the extra drop made by the packets. Wait for the tip to stop wobbling before you read it.
flow.context: In this step, you hang the first packet and measure how much the ruler bends.

flow.do: Add the packets one at a time. Measure the drop for 1, 2, 3 and 4 packets. Draw a graph with the load along the bottom and the drop up the side. Draw a line through the dots.
flow.say: Add one packet at a time. Measure the drop each time. Plot the dots on squared paper. Do they fall in a line? Draw a line through them.
flow.kid: Add packets one at a time. Measure the drop each time. Plot the dots.

check.q: The drop is 4 mm for 1 packet, 8 mm for 2 packets and 12 mm for 3 packets. What drop do you expect for 4 packets?
check.why: The drop grows by 4 mm for each packet. So four packets give about 16 mm. The answer 20 mm adds too much. The answer 8 mm looks at the early numbers only. This even growth is why a bending ruler can be a force meter.

flow.context: In this step, you add the packets one by one and draw the graph that turns your ruler into a scale.

flow.do: On day 2, hang an apple in the bag. Measure the drop from the empty bag. Find that drop on your graph. Go across to the line and down to the load in newtons. Do the same for the other two objects.
flow.say: Day two. Hang the apple. How far did the tip drop? Find that drop on the side of your graph. Go across to the line, then down to read the weight in newtons.
flow.kid: Hang the apple. Measure the drop. Use your graph to read its weight.

ask.q: How can you check that your ruler scale is right?
good: Weigh the apple on a kitchen scale and compare.
Use the packets, because I know their weight.
Check it three times and see if the answers match.

flow.parent: Check each object on a kitchen scale and divide the grams by 100 to get newtons. A difference of 10 to 20 percent is a good result for a ruler. If an object is heavier than your heaviest packet load, the graph cannot be trusted beyond it.
flow.context: In this step, you weigh three mystery objects with your ruler scale and check them.

flow.do: Compare your ruler's readings with the kitchen scale for all three objects. Write the size of each error. Ask your child what to change to make the ruler scale better.
flow.say: How close was your ruler scale? What could you change to make it better? A thinner ruler? A longer tip? A smaller step?
flow.kid: How close was your ruler scale? What could you change to make it better?
flow.think: A digital scale also bends a metal block. What do you think it has that your ruler does not?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bending Ruler Scale. You compare your ruler's readings with a kitchen scale and think about how to improve it.

challenges.title: The Gentlest Hold: carry a heavy bottle with the smallest pull
challenges.safety: Stay clear of the bottle's path and keep a soft cushion on the floor under it. If the band looks thin and pale, or the gauge goes past the 3 packet mark, take the bottle off straight away.
challenges.problem: Hang a 1 litre bottle of water, which weighs about 10 newtons, from a thread stretched between two points 1 metre apart. Make the pull in the thread as small as you can, and the bottle must stay at least 20 centimetres above the floor. Measure the pull with your rubber band gauge.
constraints: The two anchor points are on the ends of the stick, 1 metre apart and 80 centimetres above the floor.
Use only thread, string, paper clips, tape, pencils, books and the other things from the Sagging Line test.
The bottle must hang at least 20 centimetres above the floor.
The gauge must never read more than the 3 packet mark from your graph, which is about 15 newtons. If it does, stop and change the design.
Measure each design three times and take the middle value.
materials: a 1 litre bottle of water with the cap closed tightly
the stick, two chairs and tape from the Sagging Line test
the calibrated rubber band gauge and its graph (made in the Sagging Line test, so do that first)
a soft cushion for the floor
strong plastic or jute twine or thin nylon string (not sewing thread, and never kite manja)
general: A deep sag in a single thread, as deep as the 20 centimetre rule allows.
A longer loop to hang the bottle from, so the bottle can hang low without a flat line.
A thread tied from stick end to stick end with the bottle in the middle, with the thread cut a little longer than before.
creative: A prop in the middle, such as a pile of books or a pencil taped upright, that carries part of the weight.
Two threads side by side, each taking half the load, with a gauge on each.
A V-shaped hanger: hang the bottle from a short thread that splits into two, joined at points 30 centimetres either side of the middle of the line.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design. Build it and measure the pull. Change one thing at a time and measure again. Which design gave the smallest pull? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the pull in a line. You use what you learned in the Sagging Line test to hold a bottle with the smallest pull.

setup.art: A page with three sketches of ways to hold a 1 litre bottle between two points 1 metre apart: a deep sag, a prop in the middle, and two threads side by side.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: A bottle hanging in a deep sag from a stick on two chairs, the band gauge at one end, and a ruler showing 20 centimetres between the bottle and the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Build your design. Check that the bottle is 20 centimetres above the floor.

setup.art: A table with each design, three band lengths, the middle length and the pull read from the graph.
setup.caption: 3. Measure each design three times. Write the pull in a table.

flow.do: Read the problem and the constraints together. Ask your child to sketch two or three different designs. Ask which they think will give the smallest pull, and why.
flow.say: Our bottle weighs 10 newtons. How can we hold it between two points so the thread pulls as little as possible? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ways to hold the bottle. Which will pull least? Why?

ask.q: What would make the pull in the thread smaller?
good: A deeper sag, so the line is less flat.
Sharing the load between more threads.
A prop in the middle that takes some weight.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Gentlest Hold challenge. You plan your designs.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: the child designs and reads, the parent holds the stick and guards the bottle. With 2 to 4 children: each child sketches a design; build them one at a time on the same rig and compare the pulls. Typical values for a 10 N bottle: about 13 N with a 20 centimetre sag, and about 7 N with a 60 centimetre sag.

flow.do: Build your first design. Hang the bottle. Check that it is 20 centimetres above the floor. Read the band three times. Write the middle value. Look up the pull on your graph.
flow.say: Build your first design and measure the pull three times. Write the middle number, and find the pull on your graph. This is the number to beat.
flow.kid: Build your first design. Measure three times. Write the pull. This is the number to beat.
flow.parent: The bottle is heavy, so do not hang it from anything that might fall. Stay clear of its path, and keep the cushion under it. If the gauge goes past the 3 packet mark, take the bottle off straight away.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design and measure its pull.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as a deeper sag or a prop. Measure again. Do this at least twice more. Keep a table of the designs and their pulls.
flow.say: Change one thing at a time. Did the pull go up or down? Which change made the biggest difference, and why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Measure again. Did the pull go down? Write it in the table.

check.q: You make the sag deeper and the pull in the thread goes down. What is the best explanation?
options: A steeper line points more upwards, so less pull is needed to hold up the bottle
check.why: In a steep line, more of the pull points upwards, where it can hold the bottle. So the line needs to pull less. The bottle's weight has not changed. A stretched gauge would give a longer reading, not a shorter one.

flow.context: In this step, you improve your design and see which changes lower the pull.

flow.do: Pick your best design. Say why it works. Compare it with the pull for the straight-down case, where the bottle hangs from a single vertical thread. Write one sentence for each.
flow.say: Which design was best? Why? How does it compare with simply hanging the bottle straight down on one thread, where the pull is 10 newtons?
flow.kid: Pick your best design. Why does it work? How does it compare with hanging straight down?
flow.think: Can the pull in each half of a sagging line ever be smaller than half the bottle's weight?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Gentlest Hold. You pick your best design and explain it.

items.p: Which one describes a force completely?
items.why: A force needs both a size and a direction. '5 newtons' has no direction. 'To the left' has no size. Only '5 newtons to the left' has both.

items.p: In a tug of war, both teams pull with 400 N. This means that the rope must be standing still.
items.why: False. Balanced forces mean the rope does not change its motion. It may be still, or it may be moving at a steady speed. A steady speed also has a net force of zero.

items.p: A cart is pushed right with 9 N. Friction pulls it left with 4 N. The net force is ____ N to the right.
items.why: 9 take away 4 is 5. The bigger force wins, and the net force is the difference, pointing the way of the bigger force.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the distance between the two places that hold a line
how far the middle of the line dips
the pull along a rope or string held tight
what is left after adding and taking away all the forces
items.why: Span is the gap between the supports. Sag is the dip in the middle. Tension is the pull inside the line. The net force tells you which way a thing will start to move.

items.p: A 5 N bottle hangs in the middle of a line. You pull the line flatter. What happens to the pull at each end?
items.why: A flatter line points more sideways. Only the upward part of the pull can hold the bottle, so the line must pull harder. A wrong pick of 2.5 N often comes from thinking that the ends just share the weight.

items.p: Are the forces on each thing balanced or not balanced?
items: a book resting on a table
a cyclist at a steady speed
a bucket speeding down a well
items.why: A thing that is still, or moving at a steady speed, has balanced forces. A thing that speeds up, slows down or changes direction has a net force.

items.p: Hari says: 'To stop my washing line sagging, I will pull it as tight as I can.' What would you tell Hari? Use the ideas of pull and angle.
items.a: A line with a wet cloth in the middle can never be pulled straight. The flatter you pull it, the harder each end pulls, so the line may break or pull the hooks out. It is better to let the line sag a little, or to tie the ends higher and add a prop in the middle.
items.why: A strong answer says that a flatter line pulls harder on its ends, because only the upward part of the pull holds the cloth. It offers a fix, such as more sag or a prop.

items.p: On a made-up calibration graph, a band is 12 cm long for 5 N and 16 cm for 10 N. A bag stretches the band to 15 cm. About what is the pull?
items.why: 15 cm is three quarters of the way from 12 cm to 16 cm. Three quarters of the way from 5 N to 10 N is about 8.75 N, which is about 9 N. The answer 15 N mixes up centimetres with newtons.

items.p: Put these steps for calibrating a rubber band gauge in order.
a: Hang a known load and measure the band
Add more known loads and measure each one
Plot the points and draw a line through them
Hang the unknown thing and measure the band
Read the load from the graph
items.why: You must test the gauge with known loads first. Only then can the graph turn a band length into a load. Reading the unknown thing comes last.

items.p: A 5 N bottle hangs on a line that sags 10 cm. Each end pulls with about 13 N. About how many times bigger is the pull at each end than the weight of the bottle?
items.why: 13 divided by 5 is 2.6. The pull at each end is about 2.6 times the weight, although the bottle has not got any heavier.

items.p: A kitchen scale shows 3 g with nothing on it. This is called a zero error.
items.why: True. Every reading will be 3 g too big. This kind of mistake is the same each time. You can find it by checking with nothing on the scale, and you can fix it by taking 3 g off each reading.

items.p: Draw a book lying on a table. Use arrows to show its weight of 8 N and the push of the table. Use 1 cm for each 1 N. Label each arrow.
items.a: A book with an arrow 8 cm long pointing down, labelled 'weight 8 N', and an arrow 8 cm long pointing up, labelled 'push of the table 8 N'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two arrows of the same length, one pointing down and one pointing up, so the forces balance.

items.p: Ten readings of one pull go from 4.7 N to 5.3 N. What is the spread?
items.why: The spread is the gap between the smallest and the largest reading. 5.3 take away 4.7 is 0.6. The answer 5.0 is the typical value, not the spread.

items.p: A 5 N bottle is swung from the side by about 60 degrees. At the bottom of the swing, the string pulls with about double the weight. About how many newtons?
items.why: Double 5 N is 10 N. The string must turn the bottle's path upwards at the bottom, which takes extra pull.

items.p: Mala stands on a bathroom scale in a lift. The number goes up for a moment as the lift starts to move up. Has she become heavier? Explain.
items.a: No. Her weight has not changed. The lift is speeding up upwards, so the floor must push her up harder than her weight for a moment. The scale measures the push on it, so it shows a bigger number.
items.why: A strong answer says the scale measures the push of the person on it, and that a thing which is speeding up needs more push than its weight.

items.p: How does a digital kitchen scale measure a force?
opts: A thin metal pattern on a metal block stretches slightly when the block bends under the load
A spring inside stretches, and a pointer slides along a scale
A person inside looks at the weight and writes it down
items.why: A digital scale uses a strain gauge, a thin metal pattern that stretches when the block under the tray bends. A spring and a pointer are how a spring balance works. Nobody sits inside the scale.

items.p: A line holds a 10 N bottle in its middle, and each side slopes 30 degrees below the level. Each side pulls with 10 N. What would a flatter line, sloping 10 degrees, pull with?
items.why: A flatter line points more sideways, so only a thin slice of its pull holds the bottle up. The pull has to be bigger. The answer 'exactly 10 N' is only true for the 30 degree line.

items.p: Scale A reads 502 g, 502 g and 503 g for a sealed 500 g packet. Which description fits scale A best?
opts: Precise, with a small zero error of about 2 g
items.why: The readings are very close together, so the scale is precise. They are all about 2 g too big, which points to a zero error. It is very nearly accurate, but not exactly.

items.p: Scale B reads 495 g, 510 g and 503 g for the same 500 g packet. Compared with scale A, scale B is:
opts: Less precise, because its readings are more spread out
More precise, because it has a reading below 500 g
items.why: Scale B's readings are spread over 15 g. Scale A's are spread over 1 g. A smaller spread means more precise. Having one reading below the true value does not make a scale more precise.

items.p: The readings 4.8 N, 5.0 N, 5.2 N, 5.0 N and 4.9 N are lined up in order. The middle value is ____ N.
items.why: In order they are 4.8, 4.9, 5.0, 5.0, 5.2. The middle one is 5.0.

items.p: Repeating a measurement many times and taking the middle value removes a zero error.
items.why: False. A zero error is the same in every reading, so repeating does not remove it. Repeating helps with reading errors, which go up and down. A zero error is found by checking with nothing on the tool.

items.p: Is each mistake a reading error or a zero error?
items: looking at the pointer from above
a scale showing 2 g with nothing on it
a ruler with its first centimetre cut off
a forcemeter pointer that starts above 0
items.why: A reading error changes from one reading to the next. A zero error is the same each time, because the tool does not start at zero.

items.p: A band is 8 cm long with no load and 20 cm long with 15 N. It stretches evenly. How long is it with 5 N?
items.why: The band stretches 12 cm for 15 N. That is 4 cm for every 5 N. So at 5 N it is 8 plus 4, which is 12 cm.

items.p: Match each idea to what it is.
pairs: the pull along the surface of a liquid
a thin metal pattern that stretches when a block bends
a line used to read an unknown load
items.why: Each one is a way of dealing with force: a hold at a water surface, a push from sunlight, a sensor inside a scale, and a graph made from known loads.

items.p: Which of these makes a bottle on a string pull harder than its weight?
opts: Swinging through the bottom of its path
Being lowered slowly at a steady speed
items.why: At the bottom of the swing, the string has to turn the bottle's path upwards, so it pulls more than the weight. When a bottle hangs still or moves at a steady speed, the pull equals the weight.

items.p: Suspension bridges have cables that sag in a gentle curve instead of being pulled straight. Explain why, using the idea of pull and angle.
items.a: A straight cable would have to pull enormously hard to hold the weight of the bridge, because it would point mostly sideways. A cable that sags points more upwards, so it pulls less, and the towers and the cable need not be so strong.
items.why: A strong answer links the flatness of the cable to a bigger pull, and says that a sag lowers the pull for the same load.

items.p: Two children have ten readings of one pull and want to give one number.

views.who: Mina, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: I will pick the smallest reading, because that is when the band was least disturbed.

views.who: Kabir, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: I will pick the middle value of all ten, because it sits in the centre of the readings.

items.ask: Whose method is better for finding a typical value? How could you test it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer prefers the middle value, because one extreme reading can be a fluke. A test could be to repeat the ten readings again and see which method gives the same number more often.
items.why: A typical value should not depend on one odd reading. The middle value uses all the readings and is not changed by one extreme. Testing both methods on a second set of ten readings shows which is steadier.

items.p: A coin on water is held with about 0.006 N. An apple pulls down with 1 N. About how many times bigger is the apple's weight?
items.why: 1 divided by 0.006 is about 167, which is about 170. So the apple's weight is about 170 times bigger.

items.p: Why can a small fridge magnet lift a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth?
opts: Between atoms, the electric and magnetic force is far stronger than gravity
The Earth does not pull on small things
The magnet weighs more than the Earth
items.why: Gravity looks strong to us only because the Earth is so big. Between two small things, the magnetic and electric force is vastly stronger. The Earth does pull on the clip, and the magnet wins anyway.

items.p: Light has no weight, so it cannot push anything.
items.why: False. Light carries a push, called radiation pressure. It is tiny, but in space sunlight can move a thin sail.

items.p: Put these in order, for taking a trustworthy measurement.
a: Guess the answer and the reason
Line up the readings in order
items.why: A guess with a reason comes first. You then measure several times and line up the readings, choose a typical value, and report how much the readings spread.

items.p: Three forces act on a box: 6 N right, 4 N right and 3 N left. Draw all three with 1 cm for each 1 N. Then draw the net force.
items.a: Three arrows on a box: 6 cm and 4 cm pointing right, and 3 cm pointing left. The net force is an arrow 7 cm long, pointing right.
items.why: 6 plus 4 is 10 to the right, and 3 to the left takes away. 10 take away 3 is 7 N to the right.

items.p: A child on a playground swing says she feels heavier at the bottom of each swing. Is she right? Explain.
items.a: Yes, in a way. Her weight does not change. At the bottom of the swing, the chains must turn her path upwards, so they pull on her harder than her weight. The seat pushes up on her harder, and she feels it as a heavier feeling.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pull on a moving thing can be bigger than its weight, and that the seat pushes up harder at the bottom.

items.p: A rope holds a 100 N load in its middle. Each side slopes 10 degrees below the level. Roughly how hard does each side pull?
items.why: Only the upward part of each side's pull holds the load. At 10 degrees, that part is only about a sixth of the pull, so each side pulls about three times the load. The answer 50 N would be right for a rope hanging straight down, with two ropes sharing the load.

items.p: A 1 metre line has a sag of 5 cm, and each end pulls about 25 times the load. The load is 4 N. What is the pull at each end, in newtons?
items.why: 25 times 4 is 100. The bottle weighs only 4 N, and the flat line makes each end pull with 100 N.

items.p: Anjali's gauge reads 0.2 N with nothing hanging on it. She says it is small enough to ignore. A bag makes it read 3.1 N. What should she do, and why?
items.a: She should not ignore it. She should either reset the zero, or take 0.2 N off every reading, so the bag is 2.9 N. A zero error is the same each time, so leaving it makes every reading too big.
items.why: A strong answer names the zero error and says it must be subtracted from all readings, or that the zero must be reset.

items.p: Five readings of a pull are 4.9, 5.1, 5.0, 5.0 and 5.4 N. Which report is most sensible?
opts: About 5.0 N, with readings from 4.9 to 5.4 N
5.4 N, the largest, to be safe
items.why: The middle value is 5.0 N, and the readings spread from 4.9 to 5.4 N. Writing 5.08 N pretends the tool is finer than it is. Reporting only the largest ignores the other readings.

items.p: A scale that shows three decimal places must be more accurate than one that shows one decimal place.
items.why: False. The number of decimal places shows how finely a scale shows its answer, not how close the answer is to the truth. A scale with a zero error shows many wrong digits.

items.p: A 5 N bottle hangs from a string. Is the pull of the string bigger than, smaller than or equal to the weight at each moment?
items: the bottle swings through the bottom
the bottle is momentarily still at the top of a swing
the bottle is lifted at a steady speed
the hand starts to lift the bottle
the hand starts to lower the bottle
items.why: The pull equals the weight when the bottle is still or moves at a steady speed. It is bigger when the bottle speeds up upwards or turns upwards. It is smaller when the bottle starts to speed up downwards.

items.p: Priya and Sam talk about a set of ten readings of a pull.

views.who: Priya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: There is a true size of the pull. Our readings scatter around it, and better tools get us closer.

views.who: Sam, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: We never meet the true pull. We only meet our readings. The true value is just an idea in our heads.

items.ask: Which view is more useful for an engineer building a bridge? Which view is more careful about what we really know?
items.a: Answers vary. An engineer works as if there is a true value, as Priya says, because it lets them predict. Sam's view is more careful about what we actually know. Both can be right in different ways.
items.why: Priya's view helps us work. Sam's view reminds us that a measurement is all we ever have. Good thinkers can hold both.

items.p: Reading a value between two measured points on a graph is called ____.
items.why: To interpolate is to find a value between two points that you have measured, by reading along the line. It is safe inside the range of your known loads.

items.p: When the block inside a digital scale bends, what does the chip measure?
opts: A small change in how easily electricity passes through the stretched metal pattern
items.why: A stretched metal pattern is a little longer and thinner, so electricity finds it a little harder to pass. A chip measures that change and turns it into a number.

items.p: Sunlight pushes on an absorbing sail with about 5 millionths of a newton for each square metre. A sail has 100 square metres. What is the push, in newtons?
items.why: 100 times 5 millionths is 500 millionths. That is 0.0005 newtons, which is five ten-thousandths of a newton.

items.p: You need to hang a heavy wet quilt between two walls. Design the line, and explain why your design does not need a very strong rope.
items.a: Hang the line with a good sag, and tie the ends high. Add a prop in the middle, such as a pole with a fork, to carry part of the weight. A line with a sag points more upwards, so each end pulls less. A prop splits the span into two shorter parts.
items.why: A strong answer uses a sag or a prop, and explains that both reduce the pull in the line, because more of the pull points upwards.

items.p: Draw a bottle hanging in the middle of a sagging line. Show the weight and the pulls of the two sides. Make the side arrows longer than the weight arrow and say why.
items.a: A bottle with a short arrow pointing down labelled weight, and two longer arrows along the line pointing up and outwards. A note says that only the upward part of each side's pull holds the bottle, so each side pulls more than half the weight.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the pulls along the line, each with an upward part. The note should say that the sideways parts cancel each other and only the upward parts hold the weight.

items.p: A cotton thread holds a bag when pulled slowly, but snaps when jerked. What is the best explanation?
opts: For an instant, a jerk makes the pull far bigger than a steady pull
The thread gets weaker when the bag moves
The bag gets heavier when it is jerked
items.why: A moving or jerking load speeds up quickly, and that needs a much bigger pull for a short time. The thread did not change, and the weight of the bag did not change.

items.p: Put these steps for the Bending Ruler Scale in order.
a: Fix the ruler under a book with its tip over the table edge
Hang packets of known weight and measure the drop
Plot the drops and draw a line
Hang a mystery object and measure the drop
Read its weight from the graph and check it on a kitchen scale
items.why: The ruler must be fixed first. You calibrate it with known loads and draw the graph before weighing a mystery object. The check at the end tells you how good the scale is.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A spring balance, a strain gauge, a bending ruler and a mercury thermometer.
items.a: The mercury thermometer, because it measures temperature. The other three can be used to measure force.
items.why: A spring balance stretches, a strain gauge bends and a ruler bends, so all three can show a force. A thermometer shows how warm something is.

quiz.p: In a drawing of forces, what does the length of an arrow show?
quiz.why: The arrow's length shows the size of the force, and its point shows the direction. A long arrow stands for a big force.

quiz.p: Two children push a box right with 10 N and 14 N. A third child pulls it left with 4 N. What is the net force?
quiz.why: 10 plus 14 is 24 to the right, and 4 to the left takes away. 24 take away 4 is 20 N to the right. The answer 28 N adds the 4 instead of taking it away.

quiz.p: A trolley moves along a smooth floor at a steady speed. What is true about the forces on it?
opts: There is a net force forwards
There is no friction at all
quiz.why: A thing moving at a steady speed has balanced forces. If there were a net force forwards, it would speed up. Friction may still be there, balanced by a push.

quiz.p: A rope holds a heavy load in its middle. Which change makes the pull in the rope smaller?
quiz.why: A rope with a bigger sag points more upwards, so it needs to pull less. Pulling it tighter makes it flatter, which raises the pull. A swinging load can make the pull bigger.

quiz.p: Why can no washing line be pulled perfectly straight with a wet saree in the middle?
opts: It would need an endless pull
The line is made of the wrong material
quiz.why: As the line gets flatter, the pull needed grows without limit. A perfectly straight line would need an endless pull, which no rope can give.

quiz.p: Why do we hang loads that we already know on a rubber band before using it as a gauge?
opts: So that we can make a graph that turns band lengths into newtons
So that the band gets warm
So that the band becomes stronger
quiz.why: The known loads let us plot the length for each pull. The graph is then used to read unknown pulls. Hanging loads does not warm or strengthen the band.

quiz.p: Why should you not trust the graph far beyond your last known load?
opts: The band may stop stretching evenly, or snap
quiz.why: A rubber band follows a neat pattern for small loads only. Past the loads you tested, you do not know how it behaves, and it might break.

quiz.p: Why do scientists measure the same thing several times?
opts: Readings vary a little, and several readings show the spread and the typical value
To make the first reading true
quiz.why: No reading is exact. Several readings show how much the numbers spread, and the middle value is a more trustworthy answer than one reading alone.

quiz.p: A scale shows 2 g with nothing on it. You put a potato on it and read 152 g. What does the potato weigh?
quiz.why: The 2 g is a zero error that is in every reading. Taking it away gives 150 g. The answer 154 g adds it instead.

quiz.p: A bathroom scale in a lift shows a smaller number for a moment. What is the lift doing?
quiz.why: When a lift starts to go down, the floor pushes up on you with less than your weight for a moment. A scale under you reads less. Starting to move up makes it read more.

quiz.p: What does a coin on the surface of water show about water?
opts: The surface pulls along itself and holds on to the coin
Water is heavier at the top
quiz.why: The surface of water acts like a thin stretched skin. This is surface tension. It is a small force, which we can measure by finding how much it takes to lift the coin off.

quiz.p: Sunlight can push a thin sail in space. Why does sunlight not push a sheet of paper across a table?
opts: The push is far too small to beat friction and the paper's weight
quiz.why: The push of sunlight is about five millionths of a newton for each square metre. On a table, friction and weight are much bigger. In space, nothing else is acting, so the tiny push adds up over time.

open_questions.q: Why is gravity so much weaker than the other forces?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure how much weaker gravity is, about a million million million million million million times weaker than the electric force between two protons. Nobody knows why.

open_questions.q: Is there a true value behind a set of readings, or only the readings?
open_questions.why_open: In everyday life, a true value is a useful idea. At the size of atoms, quantum physics suggests that some quantities have no sharp value before they are measured. How to understand this is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How small a force can we ever measure?
open_questions.why_open: Tools get better every few years, but quantum physics sets a limit on how gently any measurement can be made. Scientists are still looking for clever ways to get past it.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a gecko's foot hold on to a smooth wall with tiny forces?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree that the forces between very many tiny hairs and the wall add up. They are still working on how the grip is released so quickly.

open_questions.q: Why is the surface pull of water so large compared with most liquids?
open_questions.why_open: The pull comes from the way water particles hold on to each other. The exact details of water's behaviour at its surface are still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can sunlight alone take a spacecraft to the stars?
open_questions.why_open: Small solar sails have flown in space, but a sail big enough and light enough to travel far has not been built. Whether we can build one is an open engineering question.

jokes.j: Why was the force arrow so honest?

jokes.a: It was carrying the weight of the world, and then some.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of made-up results from the Sagging Line test. How many centimetres does the band stretch for each extra 5 N? Where does the pattern change?
maths.explain: From 0 to 5 N, the band goes from 8 to 12 centimetres, which is 4. From 5 to 10 N, it goes from 12 to 16, which is 4. From 10 to 15 N, it goes from 16 to 20.5, which is 4.5. The steps grow a little at the end, so the band is starting to stretch more easily.
maths.context: In the Sagging Line test, you hang packets of 5 N on a rubber band and draw a graph. This graph shows made-up results.

chart.title: Length of the band for each load (made-up numbers)

maths.why_maths: Taking away neighbouring numbers on a graph shows whether the steps are even. Even steps tell you that a band can be used as a gauge.

maths.problem: A 5 N bottle makes each end of a 1 metre line pull with about 6 N when the sag is 25 centimetres, and about 13 N when the sag is 10 centimetres. How many times bigger is the second pull than the first? Round to one decimal place.
maths.explain: 13 divided by 6 is about 2.2. The sag fell from 25 to 10 centimetres, which is 2.5 times smaller, and the pull rose about 2.2 times. So the pull rises nearly as fast as the sag falls.
maths.context: In the Sagging Line test, you measure the pull at the end of a line at three different sags.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two pulls as a ratio shows how fast the pull grows when the line gets flatter, which a plain subtraction does not show.

maths.problem: A 1 metre line has a sag of 2 cm, and each end pulls about 12.5 times the load. The load is 8 N. Would a thread that breaks at a pull of 60 N hold?
maths.explain: 12.5 times 8 is 100. The thread breaks at 60 N, and the pull is 100 N, so it would snap. Letting the line sag more would lower the pull.
maths.context: In the Sagging Line test, the flatter the line, the more times the load each end pulls.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the load by the pull ratio predicts whether a thread will break, before you hang the weight.

maths.problem: A coin needed 30 grains of rice to pull it off plain water, and 12 grains to pull it off soapy water. Each grain weighs 0.02 grams. What is the difference in the pull, in grams? How many times bigger is the plain-water pull?
maths.answer: The difference is 0.36 grams. The plain-water pull is 2.5 times bigger.
maths.explain: 30 times 0.02 is 0.6 grams. 12 times 0.02 is 0.24 grams. 0.6 take away 0.24 is 0.36 grams. 30 divided by 12 is 2.5.
maths.context: In the Button and the Water test, you drop rice grains into a pan until a coin pulls off the water, first plain and then with soap.
maths.why_maths: Turning counts into grams, and comparing them with a ratio, lets you say how much soap changed the water's hold.

maths.problem: In a drawing, 1 centimetre stands for 10 N. Team A's arrow in a tug of war is 4.5 centimetres long. Team B's arrow is 3.8 centimetres long. How many newtons does each team pull with? Who wins, and by how many newtons?
maths.answer: Team A pulls with 45 N and Team B with 38 N. Team A wins by 7 N.
maths.explain: 4.5 times 10 is 45. 3.8 times 10 is 38. 45 take away 38 is 7. The net force is 7 N towards Team A.
maths.context: You draw force arrows with a chosen scale, such as 1 centimetre for 10 newtons. This is a tug of war drawn that way.
maths.why_maths: A scale turns a length on paper into a force. Subtracting the two forces then gives the net force.

maths.problem: Ten readings of a pull, in newtons, are 4.8, 5.0, 5.2, 4.9, 5.0, 5.1, 5.0, 4.7, 5.0 and 5.3. What is the spread? Add them up and divide by 10 to find the mean. Is it close to the middle value?
maths.answer: The spread is 0.6 N. The mean is 5.0 N, the same as the middle value.
maths.explain: The smallest is 4.7 and the largest is 5.3. 5.3 take away 4.7 is 0.6. The sum is 50.0, and 50.0 divided by 10 is 5.0. The middle value of the ordered list is also 5.0.
maths.context: In Ten Readings, One Pull, you read the same band ten times and look at the spread of your numbers.
maths.why_maths: The spread and the mean are two ways of describing a set of readings, so you can give one honest answer instead of ten.

maths.problem: A kitchen scale shows 3 grams with nothing on it. You put a mango on it and it shows 287 grams. Then you put on a second mango and the scale shows 571 grams. How much does each mango weigh? What does the second weighing tell you?
maths.answer: The first mango weighs 284 grams and the two mangoes weigh 568 grams together. The second mango weighs 284 grams.
maths.explain: 287 take away 3 is 284. 571 take away 3 is 568. 568 take away 284 is 284. The two mangoes weigh the same. The zero error of 3 grams is taken away once from every reading.
maths.context: A scale with a zero error shows a number that is too big each time, by the same amount.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the zero error from every reading shows the true weights and lets you compare the mangoes honestly.

maths.problem: A lorry full of sugar cane weighs 31.7 tonnes on the weighbridge on the way in. After the cane is unloaded, it weighs 12.4 tonnes on the way out. How many tonnes of cane were on the lorry? How many kilograms is that? About how many newtons does that cane weigh?
maths.answer: 19.3 tonnes, which is 19,300 kilograms. It weighs about 193,000 newtons.
maths.explain: 31.7 take away 12.4 is 19.3 tonnes. One tonne is 1000 kilograms, so 19.3 tonnes is 19,300 kilograms. Each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons, so 19,300 times 10 is 193,000 newtons.
maths.context: In Be a Weighbridge, you weigh yourself with and without a bag and subtract. A weighbridge does the same for a lorry.
maths.why_maths: Weighing twice and subtracting gives the weight of the cargo alone. Changing tonnes to kilograms and newtons shows the size of the force.

how_we_found_out.story: In the late 1800s, many scientists treated the pull of a water surface as one fixed number for clean water. Agnes Pockels was born in 1862 in Venice and grew up in Braunschweig in Germany. Girls were not allowed to go to a university, so she learned physics from her younger brother's textbooks. In her kitchen, while washing dishes, she noticed that grease changed how a water surface behaved. She hung a button from one arm of a simple balance and added weights to the other side, until the button was pulled off the water. This measured a tiny force without a laboratory. She found that a clean surface pulled steadily, and that a film of oil made the pull much smaller. In January 1891, she wrote to the English scientist Lord Rayleigh. He saw how good her work was, and he helped to get her letter printed in the journal Nature that year. Later, scientists used troughs like hers to study thin films.
how_we_found_out.who: Agnes Pockels (1862 to 1935), a German scientist who taught herself physics, and Lord Rayleigh, who helped to publish her work
how_we_found_out.when: She wrote her letter in January 1891, and Nature printed it in 1891
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people treated the surface of water as a single fixed thing, with one pull that did not depend on what was on it. Pockels showed that a thin film of oil changes the pull a lot. She did it by measuring it, with a button, a balance and a basin of water.

roots.context: We have drawn forces as arrows, hung a bottle on a sagging line and measured the hold of water on a coin. Now we ask what these measurements tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A 5-newton bottle on a nearly flat line made each end pull with about 13 newtons. A pull that holds something up can be far bigger than its weight. That bigger pull hides inside the line. So the size of a force is not set by the load alone.
deep_truth.habit: We think a support only has to be as strong as the weight it carries, so we read the strength of a rope off its load. That leaves out the angle, which can change the pull by a large amount.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sagging Line test, the band gauge showed a pull of about 13 newtons at each end when the sag was 10 centimetres, for a bottle of about 5 newtons. If your own numbers differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your muscles often pull many times harder than the weight you hold, because of the angles of your bones. Your body is full of strong pulls that go unnoticed.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings use curves to keep pulls small. A spider's web hangs in loose curves, and a branch bends in the wind instead of staying stiff.
three.what_is_this_world: A thing that looks calm can be full of strong pulls. Rest is often a balance of big forces, and the angles decide how big they are.

roots.thread: Every pull we measured has the same source in the end. The line, the band and the skin of water pull because their atoms hold on to each other with the electric force. That one force shows itself as a rope's tension, a band's stretch and a water surface's hold. The pull of the Earth is the odd one out, and nobody yet knows why gravity is so much weaker than the rest.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha reminded a musician named Sona of his lute. If its strings are too tight, they snap and give no music. If they are too slack, they give no music either. When the strings are tuned evenly, the lute sings.
teachings.link: A line pulled too tight carries too much pull, and one with no sag cannot hold at all. A sag in the right place makes it last.

teachings.teaching: What is stiff and unbending breaks. What is soft and yielding lasts. A tree that will not bend is easily broken.
teachings.link: The tight rope snapped, and the rope with a curve held through the monsoon.

science.text: The electric force between atoms explains tension, stretch and surface tension. Gravity is the one everyday force that is different.
Why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces is not known.

other_view.view: Safe structures come from strong materials and large safety margins. If every part is strong enough, the angles do not matter much, and talk of balance is poetry.

practice.title: Feel the pull grow as the line goes flat
practice.say: Hold a thread between your two hands. Hang a key in the middle. Start with your hands close together, so the thread sags deeply. playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Sagging Line test needs a stick of about 1 metre, two heavy chairs and a wide rubber band. Bands differ a lot. If three 500 gram packets stretch your band to more than about four times its relaxed length, or the band looks thin and pale, use two bands side by side or a stronger one. The calculated pulls (about 6, 9 and 13 newtons for 25, 15 and 10 centimetre sags with a 5 newton bottle) hold for a span of 1 metre, and real numbers will be a little different. The Button and the Water test is the most delicate: the coin must hang flat, and the usual result is roughly 10 to 60 rice grains for plain water, with clearly fewer for soapy water. It may take two or three tries to get a coin that hangs level, and a greasy coin or a tilted coin gives a small number. The ruler in the Bending Ruler Scale must be firmly pinned, and the bend per packet depends on the ruler, so slide it until one packet bends it by 3 to 10 millimetres. The Swinging Bottle needs a grown-up to release the bottle and a soft cushion on the floor. Digital bathroom scales may freeze their first reading, so step on again for each reading. Facts to check before use: the details of Agnes Pockels' life, Anna Mani's career, the solar sail missions and the strain gauge history. Feasibility review: the Sagging Line pulls were checked by the usual cable formula; the rice grain count for the water test (about 20 to 40) is a typical estimate and the coin must hang level; magnet strength and ruler stiffness vary a lot between homes.

If you measure carefully, you should get exactly the same number every time.
Eye position, small wobbles and how you hold the tool change a reading a little each time.
Ten careful readings of the same thing can all be a little different.
Every reading has small errors, so repeated readings spread out, and we choose a typical value.
A scale that shows more digits is always more accurate.
Digits show how finely a scale reads, not how close the reading is to the true value.
A scale that always shows 3 grams too much can still give nearly the same reading each time.
That scale is precise but not accurate, because its zero error shifts every reading by the same amount.
Your weight on a scale stays the same however you move.
A scale measures how hard you push on it, and bending your knees fast changes that push.
Light pushes on what it hits, though the push is very small.
Light carries a tiny push called radiation pressure, even though it has no weight.
Two forces pointing opposite ways along one line partly cancel each other.
Opposite forces take away from each other, and what is left is the net force.
A gauge can be trusted for loads far heavier than any it was tested with.
A tool can only be trusted inside the range where it was checked against known loads.
odd: Push, pull and tension are forces that need a direction as well as a size; mass needs only a size.

In the first three the forces cancel; a speeding-up car has unbalanced forces, so its motion changes.
In the first three a scale shows the true weight; speeding up changes how hard you push on it.
